# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-22

Toronto 26-6-0, 56 pts after 34 games.

## Role coverage

The deadline is days out and the coach has flagged two holes he cannot plug himself: toughness and faceoffs. The coverage sheet confirms both, and checking turns out thinner than it reads because the best checkers aren't dressed.

**Toughness** is the hardest gap. Zero players at 80+, best in the room is Roberts at 73 and McCabe at 73 (shipped; the coach sees 70 on McCabe's screen today, a few points down with current form). Tucker at 70 TOUG is the best internal option and he isn't even lined. There is no way to fix this from inside the roster. Jackman (90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.70M) is the only player on the board who closes it, and the trade is already in motion. Bell (CHI, 93 TOUG, 24, $0.90M, two years) is the fallback.

**Faceoffs** has one player above 80: Sundin at 90. He is 33 and carries every draw in the building. Chlup at 75 is the next best and he is 18, a project not a fix. Holden at 71 isn't lined. Sillinger (FACE 96) or Conroy (FACE 93) would give Sundin a partner on the second and third centres. Both are already on the target list at second-round prices.

**Checking** reads six at 80+ on paper, but Tucker (83 CHKG, 29) and Svehla (83 CHKG, 35) are not in any unit. Lined, the count is three: McCabe 86 (29), Fischer 82 (24), Upshall 80 (21). Fischer's production has collapsed from 0.63 to 0.22 pts/g while his ice rose from 20.8 to 22.3 minutes, which makes him a question mark rather than an answer. Dressing Tucker lifts lined checkers to four and is the cheapest fix available. But look at the age curve: Roberts 38, Svehla 35, and Fischer stalling means even this role has a thinning back end.

**Scoring, playmaking, speed, stamina, clutch** are all well covered with young players at the top. Gaborik at 22, Afinogenov at 25, Richards at 24, Spacek at 19 carry the 80+ weight alongside the veterans. No action needed.

**Goalies** are a trajectory question, not a coverage question. Belfour (39, $6.50M, 2.57 GAA, 0.907 SV) and Aebischer (26, $0.50M, 2.62 GAA, 0.898 SV) are a solid one-two right now. Tellqvist at 0.865 is third-string only. Belfour expires at 39, and Aebischer at 0.898 has not shown he can carry 65 games. That's a summer conversation, not a deadline one.

**The age curve across roles is the real risk.** Roberts (38), Mogilny (35), Svehla (35), and Sundin (33) anchor scoring, checking, toughness, and faceoffs. Within two years, three of those four are likely gone. The young core replaces the scoring and speed. The gaps that remain, checking depth, toughness, and faceoffs, are exactly what Jackman, Sillinger, and Chlup's development are supposed to fill.

## Trajectory

**The question this phase answers:** Does this roster age into a cliff, and can the money absorb the answer? The answer is that the age shape is correct for a contender building toward sustained success, but a $28.6M contract wave in one summer is the cliff, not the age curve itself. The money works today but compresses sharply if the re-signing wave is handled poorly.

**The age curve** shows 14 players at 23 or under, 11 at 24–29, only 3 at 30–33, and 4 at 34+. The 30–33 band is thin with three names (Sundin 33, Salo 30, Renberg 32), and all four veterans above 34 expire this summer. By July 2005, Belfour, Mogilny, Svehla, and Roberts are all gone, taking $18.3M in salary and a decade of playoff experience with them. That is intentional, and the 5–7 veteran shape from the manual will re-form once the current 24–26 group (Kaberle, Holden, Pilar, St. Jacques, Fischer) matures into it. The gap lasts one year if nothing goes wrong.

**Gaborik** is the single most urgent number on this sheet. 51 points in 34 games at 22 years old, on $1.10M with one year remaining. Every game he plays from now to July raises his asking price. If you let the season finish before locking him, you are paying his 75-game value instead of his 40-game value. Same logic for **Nash** (30 points, 20 years old, $1.20M) and **Richards** (38 points, 24, $1.00M). These three are the spine of the next five years and their current salaries will never be this low again.

**Kaberle** at 26 on $1.90M with one year left is the blueliner that bridges the age gap. He is not the highest-upside defender (75 POTE, behind Eminger's 99 and Colaiacovo's 99), but at 26 with 34 games played and 18 points, he is the only defenceman providing both immediate production and term potential. Without him, the blueline is McCabe (29) plus a collection of 21-to-24-year-olds. Lock him on five years.

**Belfour** at 39, $6.50M, and CONS 50 is the deadline decision the Coach's report doesn't address but the trajectory requires. If kept through the playoffs and then released, the club has zero proven NHL goalies for 2005–06 (Tellqvist has 7 games, Aebischer 19). If traded at the deadline for a pick using the above-80 expiring mechanic, the team loses its playoff goalie. The safest path: keep him through the playoffs, and in summer either sign a mid-70s free-agent backup or develop Aebischer (26, $0.50M, 90 POTE) with a veteran mentor signing.

**The money** works today: $66.97M payroll against $63.56M revenue but $27.93M profit, so TV and prestige income carry the gap. After the deadline (Mogilny out at $5.50M, Jackman in at $0.70M), payroll drops to roughly $62M. The summer re-signing of the 13 young players currently at $15.7M combined will likely push their total to $25–30M at market, meaning the payroll rises back to $75–80M. At $27.93M current profit, absorbing $10–15M more is possible but tight. The staggering of deal lengths prevents a 2007 cliff, but only if the 2005 wave is managed now rather than in July.

**Draft capital:** the Detroit first (round 1) is the team's only premium asset and should not be spent before the summer. The deadline deals are priced at second-round level (Jackman for Mogilny plus R2) and fourth (Sutton for Safronov plus R4), which is correct: the DET first is insurance for a summer star acquisition or a re-signing failure. The three TOR picks in rounds 2–4 are adequate depth picks.

## Calendar

The question this phase answers is whether a 26-6-0 club buys or sells at the deadline, and what to do with the 17 contracts worth $28.6M that walk in the spring. Short version: we buy for need at the deadline while shedding the veterans we will not keep, and we lock the young core on staggered long deals in the summer so the cluster never renews at once.

**We are buyers.** Toronto sit first in the East at 56 points, eight clear of NYR at 48, with only eight of 15 making the field. The coach's two holes set the buy list: toughness, where the roster best is 70 (McCabe), and the faceoff draw, where only Sundin at 87 clears 80. Buy for need, and buy for term, not rental.

**Jackman** is the primary toughness fix. STL are 8-17-2 and pressed. He reads 83 overall with 90 TOUG and 91 CHKG, 23 years old, three years left at $0.70M. A second-round price for a three-year player is the clean buy; he is not a rental we rent and lose.

**Sutton** is the D-side toughness target. ATL are 8-18-2 and rebuilding around Bouwmeester, with no reason to keep him: 92 TOUG, 88 CHKG, 76 overall, 27, four years at $1.34M. Safronov plus a fourth-rounder is the package.

**Sillinger** wins the draw at 96 FACE for PHX. A rental priced near a second-round pick is worth two playoff rounds of controlling the puck, behind Sundin, with Conroy (93 FACE, CGY) as the fallback.

**Mogilny** funds all three. The coach has already pulled him off the first line, and at 95 overall on $5.5M we will not re-sign him, so the above-80 mechanic prices him like a first-rounder. The cleanest path is Mogilny to STL for Jackman plus the second-rounder; STL get the veteran scorer they want for the rebuild.

**Belfour** is the keep-versus-move call. At 39 and $6.5M expiring he is the mechanic candidate, but he is the Cup starter and the manual says check the goalies. Keep him through the playoffs, then offer two years at $3.5-4M; move him only if the backup is ready.

For the spring, go down the expiring list. Four stars get the 5-6 year lock now, because renewing them yearly only ratchets their demands: **Gaborik** (RW 22, $1.10M), **Richards** (C 24, $1.00M), **Kaberle** (D 26, $1.90M), **Nash** (LW 20, $1.20M). Stagger the start dates so these four do not all come up together.

**Colaiacovo** (D 21, $1.10M) belongs in the lock tier on a 5-year deal: the young top-four blueliner to lock while the money is cheap.

The depth tier renews on 2-3 years at terms that break the summer cluster: **Upshall, Chistov, Smirnov, Eminger, Alexeev, Holden.** Short enough to stay cheap, long enough to end the same-summer trap on the $28.6M block.

The older tier is renew-short or let go. **Belfour** two years at $3.5-4M, or a pick via the mechanic. **Svehla** (D 35, $3.60M), **Roberts** (LW 38, $2.70M) and **Renberg** (LW 32, $2.00M) walk unless a short 2-year helps a thin spot; if any of the three reads above 80 overall, move him before expiry for a pick rather than lose him free.

**Goalies, the check.** With Belfour gone by the next summer, renew **Tellqvist** (25, $0.80M) or **Aebischer** (26, $0.50M) on a real deal as the successor, and that is the case for adding a backup goalie at the deadline rather than trusting an expiring two-deep.

## League scan

The question this phase answers: who on the other 29 clubs fills the toughness and faceoff gaps at a price Toronto can pay before Friday's deadline, and which of those clubs has a reason to say yes.

**Barret Jackman** remains the primary. STL are 8-18-2, the second-worst record in the West, with only $11.29M profit (the thinnest among sellers) and nine expiring deals. His current screen reads 79 overall with 87 CHKG, 86 TOUG, 90 POTE, 90 SPEE at 23 years old on $0.70M with three years left. STL need a veteran scorer for the rebuild and Mogilny at 95 overall prices as first-round weight even at 35. The deal is alive.

**Robyn Regehr** is the new one the data surfaced that the old target list missed. CGY are 9-20-3, the worst record in the West. 72 overall, 91 CHKG, 82 TOUG, 24 years old, $1.26M with three years of term. CGY have $12.62M profit but prestige of only 354 and zero playoff history; they are not financially desperate but they have no reason to keep a 24-year-old D on a nine-win team when they could flip him for a forward or a pick. He is the fallback if Jackman stalls, priced higher (third-rounder plus a depth forward) because of the term.

**Mike Sillinger** stays the faceoff priority. PHX are 13-17-4 at 32 points, eight out of a playoff spot. 88 overall, FACE 96, 27 points in 26 games, 33 years old, $1.8M expiring. Fourteen players expire for Phoenix. They will shed salary and collect picks. The R3 price is correct.

**Craig Conroy** is the faceoff fallback if Sillinger stalls. CGY are 9-20-3, same club, same sell logic. 80 overall, FACE 91, 41 points in 34 games, 33, $2.0M expiring. Ten players expire for Calgary. He is a rental only, so the price is R3 plus nothing, or R4 plus a young depth player. He is less valuable than Sillinger because he brings fewer points and costs more.

**Kyle Wanvig** is the one the old list missed entirely. MIN are 10-21-1 at 27 points. 71 overall, POTE 95, 86 CHKG, 85 TOUG, 23 years old, $0.60M expiring. He fills the toughness gap at 85 while carrying elite potential. Minnesota's $32.58M profit is the highest in the league, so they are not desperate, but a nine-win team has no reason to keep a 23-year-old winger on an expiring deal when he is not yet a regular producer. A late-round pick or a depth player gets him.

**Eric Belanger** is the budget faceoff fix. LA are 8-15-5 at 31 points. 72 overall, FACE 90, 27 years old, $0.70M expiring. Only 7 points in 33 games, so he is a pure draw-winning specialist, not a scorer. If Sillinger and Conroy both stall, Belanger costs a sixth-rounder and fills a role nobody else on the roster carries.

**Ramzi Abid** is a depth piece with upside. PIT are 9-16-5. 74 overall, POTE 95, 83 CHKG, 83 TOUG, 24, $0.40M expiring, 39 points in 33 games. He is not a toughness fix at the top but he dresses on a checker's line and carries 83 in both grades. Pittsburgh have 14 players expiring and $13.86M profit. A fourth-rounder gets him.

**What I would not do:** Chase Chara (OTT, 80 ovr, 89 CHKG, 88 TOUG, 27, $1.7M). Ottawa at 34 points are holding 8th in the East; the note from 2004-12-15 confirmed they are in the race. Lapointe (BOS, 88 TOUG, $5.0M, 31) and Brashear (PHI, 88 TOUG, $2.1M, 32) are too expensive or too old for a deadline rental that won't be re-signed.

## Trade construction

The question this phase answers: what do we hand STL, PHX and ATL to close the toughness and faceoff holes by Friday, and why would they say yes? Three proposals, ranked, together net a $2.56M payroll reduction and fill both gaps the coach flagged. They are not independent: if Jackman stalls, the entire toughness plan shifts.

**Jackman for Mogilny plus R2** is the primary. We send Mogilny (35, $5.50M, two years, 95 overall, 44 points in 31 games) and our own second-round pick to St. Louis. Jackman (23, $0.70M, three years, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG) comes to Toronto. Payroll swings $4.80M in our favour. STL at 8-18-2 have nine expiring deals and only $11.29M profit, the thinnest among the selling clubs. The reason they say yes is Mogilny: 95 overall and 44 points in 31 games is still a first-line winger who could score 70 in a full season, and Bouwmeester needs a veteran scorer to build around. They could flip Mogilny in July for more picks if the fit fails. The reason they say no is the $5.50M salary against $11.29M profit; if their GM's AI balks at that number, the deal is dead. Acceptance uncertain on the money.

**Sillinger for R3** is the cleanest deal on the board. We send our own third-round pick to Phoenix. Sillinger (33, $1.80M, one year, FACE 96, 27 points in 26 games) arrives as an expiring rental. Payroll rises $1.80M for four months, then clears. PHX are 13-17-4, eight out of the playoff race, with 14 contracts expiring. They are shedding in every direction and a third-rounder for a 33-year-old on an expiring deal is exactly what a seller takes. The only friction is that 27 points in 26 games shows he still produces; their GM may want a second. Accept the R3 if offered, consider R2 only if the coach confirms the faceoff gap is the one he cannot live without in the playoffs.

**Sutton for Safronov plus R4** is the cheapest and answers the coach's direct question. He asked us to name Safronov in or out by the deadline. This deal puts him out. We send Safronov (23, $0.90M, three years, 91 POTE, 3 games played) and our fourth-round pick to Atlanta. Sutton (27, $1.34M, four years, 92 TOUG, 88 CHKG) arrives. Payroll rises $0.44M, trivial. ATL are 8-18-2 rebuilding around Bouwmeester with no reason to keep a 76-overall depth defenceman when they can get a 23-year-old with 91 potential plus a pick. Safronov's ice time in Toronto is three games; he is surplus. Atlanta's prestige and record give them no reason to say no to upside. This is the highest-confidence deal of the three.

**Combined effect if all three land:** payroll drops $2.56M, toughness jumps from a best of 73 to Jackman at 90 and Sutton at 92, faceoffs gain Sillinger at 96 alongside Sundin at 90. Fischer's pairing, which the coach flagged as stalling at 0.22 pts/g on 22.3 minutes, gets Jackman alongside him, which either lifts Fischer or makes the case to drop him further down. The Detroit first-round pick stays untouched for the summer.

**If Jackman stalls, do not chase Bell at CHI.** Chicago are 6-18-6 but profitable at $22.88M; they have no financial pressure and 93 TOUG at $0.90M is something a non-desperate GM keeps. The real fallback is dressing Tucker tonight (92 CHKG, 88 TOUG, 29, $1.30M, 3 games played) and accepting toughness in the low 80s instead of the low 90s. That is not a failure; it is a playoff rotation that survives. If the coach needs more, Wanvig (MIN, 23, $0.60M expiring, 86 CHKG, 85 TOUG, POTE 95) costs a fourth-rounder at most and Minnesota's $32.58M profit means their GM has no pressure to keep a nine-win-team winger.

**If Sillinger stalls, go to Conroy (CGY, FACE 91, $2.00M expiring, 41 points in 34 games).** Calgary are 9-20-3 with ten contracts expiring. He is more points and more salary than Sillinger, so the price should be R4 rather than R3. If both faceoff deals fail, Sundin at 90 wins draws on one line and Chlup at 75 develops on the second through the playoffs. That is a problem in round one, not in the regular season.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-20
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-20

Next game vs STL on Tuesday 21 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question is who has earned more ice and who has earned less, and the answer is that three of our young guys are producing at rates that should force their minutes up while two others have been scratched for the right reasons.

**Nash** is the standout. 30 points in 33 games at 13.0 MPG is 0.91 points per game, the best rate on the roster outside Gaborik. He's playing third-line minutes while Sundin and Mogilny slow down on the top six. At 20 years old with 95 potential, he's ready for second-line ice. Move him up tonight.

**Chlup** at 18 is putting up 18 points in 22 games at 11.8 MPG on the third line. That's 0.82 per game. He's also our only centre besides Sundin who can dress. His ice time is too low for what he's giving us; he needs 14 or 15 a night to grow into the second-line centre job we'll need by February.

**Koltsov** has 14 points in 18 games at 7.6 MPG. That's 0.78 per game. He's been scratched. I don't understand it. Upshall is in ahead of him at 0.41 per game and Chistov at 0.47. Koltsov's production says he should be the fourth-line winger, not a healthy scratch.

**Spezza** and **Eminger** are scratched and I'd leave them there. Spezza is at 0.48 per game in 8.3 MPG; Eminger at 0.50 per game in 16.1 MPG on defence. Neither is producing above their minutes in a way that demands reinstatement over someone who is.

**Safronov** is the open wound. Two games, 12.5 MPG each, zero points, and he's 23 with a 91 scouting number. At 23, the development window is closing this month. Either he gets a real run before the trade deadline or the GM needs to tell me he's not in the plan.

**Smirnov** at 20 with zero games and the lowest scouting number in the group at 70 is not in the plan. That's the correct call. I see no reason to change it.

## Development trends

The trend window from December 1 to December 20 is the clearest evidence yet that this roster is splitting in two: a young core that is breaking out and a veteran top six that is collapsing faster than expected.

**Chlup** is the breakout. An 18-year-old going from 0.62 to 1.11 points per game while his ice climbed from 11.0 to 13.0 minutes. He's producing at a second-line rate in 22 games and the GM's own instruction says production wins the argument. He should be eating into the top nine, not the fourth line.

**Chistov** tripled his rate (0.29→1.00) with minutes jumping from 9.5 to 13.0. **Eminger** went 0.35→1.00 with ice climbing from 15.0 to 20.0 — that's a top-four defenceman's workload at 21. **Upshall** doubled his production (0.33→0.80) on flat minutes, meaning he's getting more out of what he's given. These three are the evidence that the pipeline is real.

**Nash** quietly went 0.83→1.11 on similar ice. **Gaborik** is holding 1.44 pts/g on 20.6 minutes, which at 22 is franchise-caliber consistency.

**Koltsov** is the young-player problem. He was 1.10 points per game in 10 games, now he's at 0.38 in 18 with minutes down from 8.7 to 6.2. Whatever happened — confidence, a demotion, something I can't see from totals — he's lost his role and his production simultaneously. At 23, this is the window where you either find a spot for him or start planning around his absence.

**Alexeev** is the same pattern at 22: 0.62→0.44 on ice down from 11.1 to 6.8. Both Koltsov and Alexeev are being squeezed off the roster by results, not by choice.

**Fischer** is the one that worries me among the near-veterans. He's 24, getting more ice (20.8→22.3), and his production collapsed from 0.63 to 0.22. That's not aging. Something about his pairing or his matchup is killing him. I'd look at whether he's been matched against the opponent's top line every night or whether his partner changed.

**Mogilny** at 1.62→0.60 is the confirmation of the earlier note, and it's worse than I expected. He's producing at a fourth-line rate while taking top-six minutes. Sundin (1.46→1.00 on 20.6 MPG) and Roberts (1.29→1.00 on 21.2) are following the same curve, just slower. Three men over 33 are getting more ice while their rate drops. The gap between what they can carry and what we're asking is widening every week.

**Safronov** finally dressed 2 games with 12.5 MPG and 0 points. The window note stands: he's being tried by default, not by plan.

No grade changes on any card in this window, so the production shifts are the only evidence we have.

## Morale watch

The room is healthy. Morale ranges from 80 to 100 with an average of 92, and the only player below 88 is a backup goalie whose minutes I cannot adjust with a line card.

**Aebischer** sits at 80, the lowest on the roster, and it has not moved. That costs him a point on every grade tonight. He has played 18 of 33 games, which is legitimate work, so this is not a minutes problem — it is a results problem or a want-to-be-the-guy problem. I cannot fix either from the bench. If his numbers are dragging from that -1 modifier, it's worth a conversation about the crease situation, but that's your call, not mine.

**Spezza** dropped 4 to 88 and is currently scratched. 14 points in 29 games at 8.3 MPG, he's producing enough to earn a spot, and sitting him will keep pulling that number down. I would dress him when the roster allows it, but 88 is not urgent tonight.

**Safronov** dropped 5 to 95. Two games played, 12.5 MPG. He's a healthy scratch most nights, and the morale model is telling me what I already know: a 23-year-old with a 91 scouting number who isn't playing is wondering why. Still at 95, so no action needed before STL.

**Sundin** is at 88, flat. 17.9 MPG for a 44-point player who should expect 20. That gap is the aging-top-six problem showing up in the ice-time model, but his morale is holding, so I'm not touching it tonight.

No one else is out of band. The room is right for Tuesday.

## Role composition

**The question here is whether each unit has the tools its assignment demands, and if not, whether I can fix it from within or need the GM's help.**

**L1 and PP1** are correct. Sundin (87 faceoffs), Roberts (81 checking), McCabe (82 checking), Fischer (82 checking) around Mogilny gives us elite skill with three 80+ defenders. PP1 has Gaborik (99 scoring, 99 playmaking) and Sundin (89 scoring, 88 playmaking) with McCabe's 82 checking as a recover option. Leave them alone.

**L2** has no one who checks above 70 except Colaiacovo's 92 on defence. Richards at 73 faceoffs is below par for a top-six centre, but Chlup is only 76 and swapping him doesn't solve it. Gaborik (97 scoring) and Afinogenov (90 scoring, 90 playmaking) are our entire offensive depth beyond Sundin. I'm not breaking this line. The cost is we lose draws on this centre and get outmuscled — that's the price of having one good scoring line.

**L3 stamina 57, clutch 59** is the concern. This line cannot carry tough minutes or be trusted in a one-goal game. Chistov's 96 speed is the only standout. Safronov carries 96 scoring but the line has no faceoff or clutch support around him. I'll manage this by keeping their assignments light, not by rebuilding the personnel.

**L4 faceoffs 52/53, checking mean 64** is a unit that can't take a draw and can't finish a check. Upshall at 81 checking is the only thing they do. But I have no better bodies to put there.

**PK1** is the one unit I want to change. Mogilny at 35 is on the first kill and dragging checking mean to 71. Tucker is scratched with 79 checking and 68 toughness. He's a better fit on the penalty kill than a fading winger, and this is a one-player swap on a four-man unit.

**Roster gaps** — unchanged from December 7th and still unsolvable from within: only one centre wins draws above 80, and best toughness on the roster is 70.

## Opponent matchup

This is a game the sheet says we should control, so the only pre-game decisions are whether to protect anyone or exploit anything, and mostly the answer is no.

**The matchup overall.** STL is 8-17-2 giving up 4.0 goals per game. We are 25-6-0 scoring 6.9 per game. Their power play is 8-for-78, which is roughly a 10 percent conversion rate, and they are 2.90 goals per game on the season. There is no unit on their side of the sheet that outclasses ours at any position.

**Their first line.** Tkachuk (86 OVR, CHKG 82, TOUG 81, FACE 90) is the one real threat. Weight at centre is 82 with FACE 74, so Sundin (FACE 87) wins that draw. Boguniecki at 78 is the weakest link on any top line we've faced all season. Roberts and Sundin handle them, and Mogilny's 91 SHPW should find soft second-pair coverage on Salvador (69 OVR, TOUG 77) and Koivisto (68 OVR).

**Their checking.** Walker (TOUG 91, CHKG 89) and McCarthy (TOUG 91, CHKG 84) are the physical options, but they're third-line and fourth-line respectively. Nash (TOUG 86, CHKG 81) is a reasonable match on the third line. Their first pair is Pronger (CHKG 81, TOUG 80) and Jackman (CHKG 87, TOUG 86), who McCabe (CHKG 83) and Fischer (CHKG 88) can handle. The toughness void is a problem against a first-line shutdown unit, and they don't have one.

**Goalie decision.** This is the only call I would make tonight. Aebischer is at 80 morale, the lowest on the roster. Belfour is 91 OVR, 95 morale, and this is an 8-17-2 opponent with a 10 percent power play and a G1 at 81 with INTE 64. Starting Belfour costs nothing in terms of result risk and gives Aebischer a breather against the weakest team we face all month.

**Lines.** No changes. The faceoff situation actually favors us more than usual: Weight (74) versus Sundin (87), Demitra (63) versus Richards (73). The only draw we lose is Cajanek (70) versus Spacek (53), and that's our fourth line against theirs. Nothing to fix.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-20
markdown:
# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-20

Toronto 25-6-0, 54 pts after 33 games.

## Role coverage

The roster at 25-6-0 is genuinely deep in speed, scoring, and clutch, but two roles are uncovered and neither can be fixed by shuffling lines.

**Toughness is missing outright.** Zero players at 80+ TOUG. The ceiling is Roberts at 73 (38 years old) and McCabe at 73 (29). Tucker at 70 is the next best and he's not lined. This cannot be solved internally — the highest toughness grade on the roster is 73, and no player under 25 carries it. Jackman (90 TOUG, 83 ovr, 23, $0.70M, three years) at the deadline is the fix, and the Mogilny-plus-second package is the price. Without it, the coach's toughness gap stays open through the playoffs.

**Faceoffs are thin to the point of being a gap.** Only Sundin (90) is above 80, and he's carrying 22-minute loads. The next-best draw man is Chlup at 75 (18), then Roberts at 75 (38). Richards is at 70. A playoff team gets out-drawn in the defensive zone against any centre in the 85+ range. Holden at 71 is not lined and not the answer. Sillinger (FACE 96, PHX) or Conroy (FACE 93, CGY) are second-round-priced rentals that solve this for the spring without long-term cost.

**Checking is thin and age-weighted.** Roberts (86, 38), McCabe (86, 29), Svehla (83, 35, not lined), Tucker (83, 29, not lined), Fischer (82, 24), Upshall (80, 21). Six names, two not lined. The coach can dress Tucker and lift this to a workable four. But Roberts at 38 is carrying the unit, and Svehla at 35 is not helping from the press box. Fischer at 82 and Upshall at 80 are the young checkers, but they are 82 and 80 — real contributors, not answer-men.

**Koltsov** at 92 speed and not lined is the clearest internal fix the coach already flagged. Moving him to third-line LW puts the team's fifth-fastest skater into the lineup and reduces the load on Mogilny (35, 94 speed) and Sundin (33, 89 speed) on the top pairs.

**Salo** at 88 scoring and not lined is the second internal waste. At 30 he's not a development project; he's a productive winger sitting out. If the coach has room on the third or fourth line, he should be in it.

## Trajectory

Is this club aging into a cliff? No. It's contract-structuring into one, and the fix is staggered extensions done this season, not next summer.

**Age shape is fine.** Fourteen players at 23 or under, eleven in their prime, seven veterans. The manual calls for 5–7 veterans and ~20 young players. Toronto hits that. The 30–33 band has three players (Sundin 33, Renberg 32, Salo 30) and two of them are on one-year deals, which is correct — you don't need long commitments in a thin band that's already been bridged by 24–29 players.

**Belfour** at 39, $6.50M, one year left, CONS 50 is the single most urgent item. Either trade for a pick using the above-80 expiring asset rule, or keep through playoffs and re-sign at $3.5–4M on two years. His value only drops after the deadline. The goalie depth behind him is a problem regardless: Tellqvist (25, $0.80M, 1y) and Aebischer (26, $0.50M, 1y) both expire the same summer. Three goalies walk at once.

**The 17-player summer** worth $28.60M is the defining risk. Of that, $14.80M is veterans (Belfour, Svehla, Roberts, Renberg) whose contracts walking is actually the club's cost relief. The remaining $13.80M is the young core (Gaborik $1.10M, Richards $1.00M, Nash $1.20M, Kaberle $1.90M, Chlup $2.34M, Upshall, Colaiacovo, Alexeev, Chistov, Spezza, Smirnov). Re-signing all of them in one off-season at market rates, when the GM is also replacing the veterans, is the payroll spike that creates the cliff three years from now.

**Chlup** at 18, $2.34M, two years left, 95 potential, already top-six is the earliest lock to do. Two years remaining means he hits UFCA at 20. A 5–6 year extension now costs a small bump and buys five seasons of control. Same logic for Nash (20, $1.20M, 1y, 95 POTE, 30 points). Gaborik at 22, $1.10M, 1y, 47 points in 33 GP is the highest-leverage extension on the roster.

**Draft capital:** Round 0 (TOR), Round 1 (DET), Round 2 (TOR), Round 3, Round 4. The DET first is ammunition the club already has and hasn't committed yet. With the Chara deal dead (Ottawa at 11-10-3, in the race), the first can either go for Jackman at a second-round price or stay as leverage for the next rebuild window. Keeping it costs nothing.

**Money:** Payroll $66.97M against revenue $61.93M and profit $28.74M. The profit number tells the GM the other revenue streams cover the gap. There is room to extend young stars at $3–5M per year each without touching the veterans' replacement budget, as long as the extensions are staggered across three summers rather than collapsed into one.

## Calendar

The calendar question is whether we hold or move between now and early March, and what happens to seventeen contracts in the summer. We are 8 points clear of second place with 49 games left, so we are unambiguously buying at the deadline. The harder work is the summer: seventeen deals worth $28.6M hit at once, and if we let them all ride we lose half our young core to the market.

**Deadline — early March, ~71 days away**

**Jackman** remains the primary buy: 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23 years old, three years at $0.70M from St. Louis (8-17-2, financially pressed). A second-round pick is the price. This is the toughness fix the Coach has flagged since November. Execute within the next three weeks; by March STL may reposition.

**Mogilny** is the primary sell: 95 overall, $5.50M, two years remaining, producing 0.75 points a game and scratched. The above-80 mechanic means he still prices as a first-round-weight asset right now. Every week he sits on the bench his value falls. Target STL or VAN who need a veteran scorer. If we land Jackman plus Mogilny back from STL, that is the cleanest path: we send the second-rounder and Mogilny to STL for Jackman, netting a one-for-one swap that sheds $4.80M and adds three years of toughness.

**Belfour** is a summer let-go (39, $6.50M, CONS 50). At 39 his overall may have slipped below 80, so the pick-for-expiring mechanic may not fire. Do not re-sign him at any price. The question is whether we keep him through April as insurance or move him in January. Keep through the deadline: if we make a deep run his experience has playoff value, and we have no proven starter behind him.

**Safronov** is a trade-by-February call. The Coach reports him a dressed scratch 31 times with morale sliding toward the 80s. His trade value falls with his morale. If we do not want him in the plan, move him by mid-February for a late pick or a high-potential depth player. If we do want him, dress him tonight and give him minutes, per the Coach's urgent request.

**Svehla** (D, 35, $3.60M) is a summer let-go. If he is above 80 overall, use the same mechanic as Mogilny and move him before March for a pick. If not, let him walk.

**Holden** (C, 26, $1.20M) is trade bait. At 26 with one year left he has market value to a contender needing a fourth-line centre. Moving him before the deadline for a late pick or prospect is better than losing him for nothing in July.

---

## Summer — the seventeen

The goal is to stagger so no more than five or six come up for renewal in any one off-season. Priority order:

**Lock 5-6 years (star tier, do this first, do not wait):**

- **Gaborik** (RW, 22, $1.10M): the team's best young forward. Must be locked before the season ends.
- **Richards** (C, 24, $1.00M): franchise centre. Same treatment.
- **Nash** (LW, 20, $1.20M): already a 20-year-old with 85 TOUG dressed on line 3. A 5-6 year deal at a modest raise is cheap insurance on a toughness core we have no other supply of.
- **Kaberle** (D, 26, $1.90M): prime-age top-pairing defenceman. Five years.

**Lock 4-5 years (developing core):**

- **Eminger** (D, 21, $1.20M): Coach says protect his pairing and his rising role. Four or five years.
- **Colaiacovo** (D, 21, $1.10M): young blueliner, needs to be part of the plan or moved. If we keep him, sign four years.

**Renew 2-3 years (depth, let them prove it):**

- **Chistov** (LW, 21, $1.10M): fourth-line role, developing. Two years.
- **Upshall** (RW, 21, $1.20M): young depth. Two years.
- **Alexeev** (RW, 22, $1.10M): Coach is moving him to 2C. If he produces there, extend to four years later; for now, two years.
- **Smirnov** (LW, 20, $0.40M): at $400K he costs nothing to retain. Two years, develops by accident or not.
- **Aebischer** (G, 26, $0.50M): third goalie. One year as insurance, then let go.

**Goalie decision (critical, per the manual's warning):**

- **Tellqvist** (G, 25, $0.80M): if he or Aebischer is going to be the starter behind Belfour, sign the chosen one to three years. The other walks. This must be decided by April, not July, or we lose both to free agency.

**Let go (do not offer):**

- **Belfour** (G, 39, $6.50M): done. Career over at this level.
- **Svehla** (D, 35, $3.60M): done. Move before deadline if above 80.
- **Roberts** (LW, 38, $2.70M): done. 38 years old on a 22-minute load.
- **Renberg** (LW, 32, $2.00M): done. Replacement-level on a $2M expiring deal.

**Trade before deadline (do not reach summer):**

- **Holden** (C, 26, $1.20M): move for a pick.
- **Safronov** (D, age unknown from this brief): move for a pick if not in the plan.

---

The net: shedding Belfour ($6.50M), Svehla ($3.60M), Roberts ($2.70M), Renberg ($2.00M), Holden ($1.20M) and possibly Mogilny ($5.50M) frees roughly $19-21M of expiring or near-expiring salary. The five priority locks (Gaborik, Richards, Nash, Kaberle, Eminger) will demand raises, but on a 22-to-26 age curve with current salaries of $1.00-1.90M those raises are manageable against the money freed. The cluster problem is solved: only five come up at once, not seventeen.

## League scan

The deadline board has three things Toronto needs: a defenceman who hits, a centre who wins draws, and a goalie for the summer after Belfour. One target answers two of those gaps at once, and a new finding on the back end changes the shape of the toughness package.

**Sutton** is the discovery of this scan. ATL's 27-year-old defenceman carries 92 TOUG, 88 CHKG and 76 overall on $1.34M with four years left. ATL are 8-18-2 with 11 expiring contracts and a $36.79M payroll they can't justify keeping intact. A defenceman with real toughness and checking who is young, cheap and under term is exactly the profile Toronto's blueline lacks, and it fills the gap above the existing pairing rather than replacing it. ATL have no reason to keep a 76-overall D when they're rebuilding around their 99-potential prospects like Bouwmeester (78 ovr, 21, same club).

**Jackman** remains the primary toughness buy and this scan doesn't change that. 83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, $0.70M, three years at STL who are 8-17-2 with the league's second-highest payroll ($56.63M) and only $12.00M profit. They must shed. Mogilny plus a second is the package. Sutton is the complement: Jackman upgrades the forward checking and toughness, Sutton does the same on the back end.

**Sillinger** is the best faceoff man available. 96 FACE, 88 overall, 90 speed, 33 years old, $1.80M, one year, at PHX who are 12-16-4 and out of the race. A second-round pick gets him for the spring. He doesn't need a long-term commitment; he needs to win draws against the opposition's top centre in June. Bates at 94 FACE, 29, $0.90M is younger and cheaper but NYI at 14-13-2 are in the race and unlikely to sell their second-best centre.

**Conroy** at 91 FACE, 80 overall, 33, $2.00M expiring from CGY (9-20-2, desperate) is the fallback if Sillinger stalls. Same price range, same rental profile.

**Miller** is the goalie target that matters for the summer. 81 ovr, 95 potential, 24, $1.00M, expiring, at BUF who are 11-14-2 and out of it. Toronto's three goalies all walk at the end of this season. If BUF won't re-sign Miller, he moves for a pick or a cheap package, and the above-80 expiring mechanic means the AI values him well even at 81. A first-round pick (the DET first) or Belfour plus a later pick gets a conversation started, though Belfour at 39 and $6.50M expiring is not something BUF wants on the ice. A straight pick-for-player deal is cleaner.

**Bell** is the toughness fallback at 93 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 85 FACE, 80 ovr, 24, $0.90M, two years. Already known, still valid. CHI are 6-18-6 but profitable at $22.88M, so they have no urgency. Only goes if Jackman fails.

**Cammalleri** is the development target worth naming but not bidding for at the deadline. 79 overall at 22 with 97 potential from a desperate LA club (8-14-5) is a prospect you'd build around, but LA's own rebuild means they'll demand a first-rounder and Toronto's DET first is better spent on Jackman or Miller.

## Trade construction

Can we fix toughness, faceoffs and the blueline with picks we already own, a player the coach wants moved, and a veteran whose decline he's already planning around? Yes, and at a payroll cost below where we sit today.

**Jackman** is the spine of this. STL at 8-17-2 with $56.63M payroll and only $12.00M profit has to shed and has to get something for a 23-year-old with three years left at $0.70M. Mogilny gives them a 95-overall anchor at 42 points in 28 games while their 18-year-old prospect develops, and the second-round pick (from TOR) is a sweetener that costs us nothing we need back. The payroll shift is $4.80M off our books and onto theirs, pushing their profit from $12.00M to roughly $7.20M. That's the acceptance risk: STL may balk at two years of $5.50M on a 35-year-old. If they do, the fallback is the second-round pick alone for Jackman, and Mogilny goes to a different desperate club (CHI at 6-18-6 has $22.88M profit and could absorb him).

**Sillinger** at 96 FACE and 88 overall from PHX (12-16-4, out of it) is the cleanest deal on the board. A third-round pick for an expiring $1.80M rental solves the faceoff gap the coverage phase flagged: we carry Sundin at 90 on 22-minute loads, and the next draw man is Chlup at 75. PHX gets a late pick for a player they won't re-sign. We add $1.80M for April and June. No term risk, no salary spike.

**Sutton** at 92 TOUG and 88 CHKG fills the D-side toughness gap the coverage phase called uncovered. ATL at 8-18-2 are rebuilding around Bouwmeester (78 ovr, 21, 99 POTE) and Sutton at 76 overall doesn't fit their core. Safronov answers the coach's explicit request to move him, and at 23 with 91 potential he's exactly what a rebuilding club values. The fourth-round pick is the sweetener. Net payroll on this deal is +$0.44M for us ($1.34M in, $0.90M out), but Safronov's morale is sliding and the coach says his trade value is time-sensitive. Move him now or lose the value.

All three together take our payroll from $66.97M to $64.41M. We get 90 TOUG, 96 FACE, and 92 TOUG on the back end while spending $2.56M less than today.

**If none land:** Bell from CHI (93 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 80 ovr, 24, $0.90M, two years) is the toughness fallback but CHI are profitable at $22.88M with no urgency. Conroy from CGY (91 FACE, 80 ovr, 33, $2.00M expiring, 9-20-2) mirrors the Sillinger logic. For the goalie gap, the above-80 expiring mechanic could send Belfour (86 ovr, $6.50M expiring) to BUF for Miller (81 ovr, 95 POTE, 24, $1.00M expiring), though the league scan notes BUF may not want a 39-year-old on $6.50M. The DET first-round pick stays uncommitted as leverage either way.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-19
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-19

Next game at TB on Sunday 19 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question is whether the young guys are getting the ice they've earned. Most of them are, but two are underused relative to their production and one decision has been left unmade long enough.

**Koltsov** has 14 points in 18 games on 7.6 minutes a night. That is 0.78 points per game on fourth-line ice. Chistov, on the third line, has 7 points in 18 games on 10.2 minutes. Koltsov is producing twice as much on a third fewer minutes. He should be on the third line.

**Alexeev** is putting up 19 points in 32 games at 10.0 MPG. Fourth-line centre minutes. That's better production than most players on the second line. He needs a promotion to a higher line. I'd put him at second-line centre where his scoring can actually matter in close games.

**Spezza** at 14 points in 29 games and 8.3 MPG is efficient but not dramatically so. His morale at 88 is the second-lowest among the young group. I'd give him the fourth-line centre role outright and stop rotating him. At 21 with a POTE of 99, he needs a fixed role to grow into, not a platoon.

**Safronov** at 23 years old with 1 game and 0 points is the one I keep raising. POTE of 91 is a real scouting number, but 3% share is not a development plan. The GM needs to name him in or out.

**Smirnov** at 20, 0 games, POTE 70. I am not pushing for him. Production is the measure the GM set, and he has none.

**Chlup** at 82 morale is the lowest among the young players. 17 points in 21 games on 11.8 MPG is fine production for an 18-year-old third-line centre. I'm watching it but making no change.

**Upshall** at 12 points in 28 games on 13.6 MPG is contributing, the GM likes him, and he's earned his current spot even if the efficiency isn't there yet. No change.

## Development trends

Over the last 18 days nobody's card moved, so the only real evidence this window is production and minutes since the first save, and that is enough to see who's climbing and who's sliding before the stretch run.

**Chlup** is the riser that matters. An 18-year-old centre at 1.12 points a game in his last 8 while his minutes crept from 11.0 to 13.0. He's out-scoring grown men on third-line ice. The plan should be building around him now, not next October.

**Upshall** and **Eminger** are the other two young guys earning more. Upshall went 0.33 to 1.00 a game on rising ice (13.4 to 15.0). Eminger, a defenceman, jumped 0.35 to 1.00 and now carries 20.0 a night. Both have taken a step; give them the same or more of the game and don't tinker with their partners.

**Klesla** (0.50 to 0.88 on flat minutes) and **Chistov** (0.29 to 0.75) are quietly climbing too. Keep their units intact and let them play.

**Koltsov** is the opposite. 1.10 a game in his first 10 is now 0.38 in his last 8, on minutes cut from 8.7 to 6.2. He's losing the job for production, not on the sheet's weaknesses, and per how we judge kids that's a fair verdict. He needs a reduced role or a scratch until he scores.

**Alexeev** slid the same way, 0.62 to 0.50 with ice halved to 6.6. **Colaiacovo** is being used less, 18.9 down to 15.9 minutes with production flat at 0.50.

**Smirnov** is 20 and has zero games across the whole window, and **Safronov** finally got one game at 23 after zero before. Two young players left to rot by default is a roster decision the GM should make on purpose, not one that happens to him.

On the veterans, the fade I flagged is holding. **Mogilny** at 35 is 0.75 a game now against 1.62 to start the season, on more ice. **Sundin** at 33 is 1.12 against 1.46 while his minutes jumped 16.9 to 21.4, and **Roberts** at 38 is 1.12 on 22.0 minutes, up from 16.5. We're loading three aging top-six players with more ice while their rate drops. **Fischer** is the one exception holding steady; 0.25 a game but that's a shutdown pair, not a decline.

## Morale watch

The room is healthy and the only clock ticking is **Safronov**, who just dropped 5 morale on a single game played all season.

**Safronov** sits at 95, down 5 from last save. He's played 1 game in 32 team games, 11 minutes in it. A 23-year-old defenceman dressed but not used is the exact profile that sours a locker room on the bench, and the drop rate says it's happening. Either he plays a real defensive role starting now or the GM needs to move him, because another 10 games at this rate puts him in the 70s where he's taking a 2-point penalty on every grade. I'd dress him and put him on the third pair immediately.

**Chlup** is at 82, unchanged, 11.8 minutes a night with 17 points in 21 games. He's 18, producing nearly a point a game on third-line minutes. His morale floor is the team's record, not his role. No minutes fix helps here.

**Aebischer** at 80 with 17 starts is the lowest number on the sheet. He's our clear #1 and already the busiest goalie. Nothing I do with lines moves him. That's a results number and will climb when the wins do.

**Spezza** dropped 4 to 88. He's 21, 14 points in 29 games, 8.3 minutes on the fourth line. The -4 is new and worth watching next save. If his calibre puts him in the 80s, he's expecting 17 a night and getting less than half that, and the model will keep squeezing him. I'll look for a chance to slide him up if a line breaks, but I won't force it today.

**Richards** at -3 to 95, 17.2 minutes, 33 points. If he's a 90+ player he wants 20 a night and 17.2 is thin, but 95 is still a comfortable number. No action.

## Role composition

The units are built correctly for what we have. The structural problem is unchanged from what I flagged on December 7th: we have three quality checkers and one faceoff centre, and they all live on the same line or the same PK unit.

**L1** is the best-balanced top line on the roster. Roberts at 80 checking and Fischer at 81 give it teeth, Sundin's 88 wins the draw, Gaborik's 96 scoring carries the offence. This line does everything asked of it. No touch.

**L2** is a possession line pretending to be a second line. Checking mean of 62 with Kaberle's 91 as the outlier means Colaiacovo, Richards and Afinogenov are all dragging that number below 60. Against a physical top pair this line gets separated from the puck. There is no arrangement of remaining players that fixes it — Tucker at 78 is the only other body who adds muscle and he's scratched for a reason. I will not restructure L2 without losing the chemistry that gives us 80 playmaking.

**L3** is a development line and the clutch mean of 59 proves it. Chlup at 75 gives the only faceoff above Richards. The scoring mean of 76 with a best of 95 says one young player is already a real threat while the others are learning. Leave it alone, let them grow.

**L4** is unusable in the draw — 52/52 across both centres means we lose every zone start on that line. No fix exists on this roster. They provide speed (87 mean) and nothing else. Short minutes for them against low-danger matchups.

**Special teams are well-arranged.** P1 enters on Sundin's 88 faceoff, then Spacek and Kaberle work the half-wall with Sundin and Roberts shooting. P2 is a speed unit with Gaborik at 96/99 and Fischer at 91. K1 pairs Roberts and Fischer's checking with Gaborik's shorty threat. K2 is a possession kill with McCabe's 81 as the anchor. I would not touch any of these.

**The roster gap remains the same one from December 7th.** Three players above 78 in checking, one above 80 in faceoffs, no one above 70 in toughness. When a physical team stacks their top line against L1 and then sends their second against L2, we have no answer. This is not a coaching adjustment. It is a trading-deadline problem.

## Opponent matchup

The question is whether TB's specific shape asks us to adjust, and the honest answer is no — their weaknesses sit exactly where our strengths already are.

**TB's defence** is the game. Boyle at 75 is their best blue-liner, and behind him it's Sarich 68, Bouillon 70, Pratt 67, Jonsson 65. Our first line — Sundin 88, Gaborik 95 with 99 speed and 99 shot accuracy, Roberts 85 — should carve that group up all night. The existing assignment is already the right one: our top unit gets the softest defence they'll see this week.

**Sundin vs Lecavalier at the dot** is a win, not a loss. Lecavalier's FACE is 60 — he's a scorer, not a centreman in the draw circle. Sundin at 88 will feed our top line offensive-zone starts against that weak blue line. The faceoff gap I flagged in December matters against teams with a true number-one centreman at the draw; Lecavalier is not that, so this particular problem doesn't apply here.

**Richards vs Andreychuk** on the second line is a draw loss (72 vs 89), but Andreychuk is 41 years old with 66 speed and 60 acceleration. Losing a faceoff against a man who can't skate is a much smaller cost. I won't break the Richards/Afinogenov/Spacek chemistry to shave 17 points of faceoff against a player who can't exploit possession anyway.

**Their physicality** is minimal. Keefe at CHKG 87 on the third line is their best checker; Lecavalier, St. Louis, and Modin all sit at 50-67 toughness. Our toughness-checking void doesn't get tested here.

**Khabibulin at 86** is the only reason this isn't a blowout. His REBC at 75 is the soft spot — high shots and second chances will rattle him.

**Start Aebischer.** His 84 overall is nine points above Tellqvist's 73, and his 86 speed handles TB's transition (St. Louis 90, Lecavalier 91) better than Tellqvist's 76.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-19

# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-19

Toronto 24-6-0, 52 pts after 32 games.

## Role coverage

**Toughness and faceoffs are the two holes in this roster, and only one of them has an internal fix.**

**Toughness.** The brief shows zero players at 80+ TOUG. The best is Roberts at 73 (38), then McCabe at 73 (29). Tucker is 70 TOUG and not lined. Even if the coach dresses Tucker, nobody on this roster finishes a check at 80. My note from December 17 says Nash carries 85 TOUG on line 3 at 20 years old, but the brief's role coverage shows him outside the 80+ bucket, which means today's displayed grade is lower than his stored grade. That gap is form, not a different player, and it still leaves the club without a reliable 80+ option. This gap cannot be fixed internally. **Jackman** (83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.70M) remains the only live target at the deadline. St. Louis are 7-16-2 and financially pressed; a second-round pick is the price.

**Faceoffs.** Sundin at FACE 90 is the only 80+ option. Chlup is next at 75, a 15-point drop, and he is 18. Holden at 71 is not lined. The coach is right that the club loses the draw on three lines every night. Internally, the coach can promote Chlup to more draws and put Holden on the fourth line, but that caps the ceiling around 75 on two lines. Externally, Sillinger (FACE 96, PHX) or Conroy (FACE 93, CGY) are second-round-priced rentals. If the GM spends a second on Jackman for toughness, a second for a faceoff man is a real cost, but the club is 24-6 and in it to win a cup, and losing draws kills playoff hockey.

**Checking.** Six at 80+ CHKG looks adequate on paper, but three of them (Svehla 35, Tucker 29, Upshall 21) are not lined. The coach can fix most of this by dressing Tucker (83 CHKG, $1.30M) nightly. Fischer at 24 with CHKG 82 is the young option. Roberts at 86 is the anchor but 38.

**Scoring and playmaking.** Covered in depth. Gaborik 92/92 (22), Sundin 92/91 (33), Afinogenov 90/87 (25), Richards 85/85 (24), Spacek 84 at 19. Mogilny at 94/93 is not lined; that is the coach's call and a trade asset, not a gap.

**Durability.** Thin. Only Roberts (98, age 38), Afinogenov (95) and Fischer (92) carry 80+. If Roberts goes down for six weeks at 38, the back end has no durable body. Spacek at 79 is close. This is a trajectory risk, not a deadline fix.

**Goalies.** Aebischer is the workhorse at 26 with 13-3, GAA 2.76, SV 0.894 in 17 games. Belfour is 39, $6.50M expiring, but still the best in net when healthy (GAA 2.57, SV 0.907 in 10 games). Tellqvist at 25 is a GAA 4.11 backup with no term. The position is covered through the playoffs; what comes after depends on whether Belfour returns and what it costs.

**The age problem underneath the coverage.** Roberts is 38, Svehla 35, Mogilny 35, Sundin 33, Belfour 39. The five best players at several positions walk after this season or the next. The young core (Gaborik 22, Richards 24, Kaberle 26, Chlup 18, Spacek 19, Fischer 24) is deep but none of them has proven at 30-plus. A role covered today by a 38-year-old is a gap in June.

## Trajectory

The question this phase answers is whether the roster ages into a cliff over three years, and the answer is no: the shape is healthy, the money is ample, and the only real danger is a contractual pile-up that the GM already has a plan to stagger.

**The age curve is fine.** Fourteen players at 23 or under, eleven at 24-29, three at 30-33, four at 34+. The manual asks for 5-7 veterans and around 20 young; Toronto has exactly that. The veterans are Belfour (39), Mogilny (35), Svehla (35), Roberts (38) at the top, and Sundin (33) as the bridge. Below them sits a genuine depth core: Nash (20), Chlup (18), Upshall (21), Colaiacovo (21), Klesla (22), Gaborik (22), Alexeev (22), Richards (24), Fisher (24), Afinogenov (25). That is a team getting younger, not older.

**The cliff is contractual, not demographic.** Seventeen players carry one year left totalling $28.60M, and among them sit the six highest-potential assets on the roster: Upshall (POTE 99), Colaiacovo (POTE 99), Nash (POTE 95), Gaborik (POTE 90), Chistov (POTE 95), Alexeev (POTE 94). Every one of them hits free agency the same summer unless the GM re-signs them. That is the summer problem already flagged and it remains the dominant planning item.

**The money is not a constraint.** Payroll $66.97M against revenue $61.93M, but profit sits at $29.56M, which means TV and other income more than covers the gap. There is room to pay Nash, Gaborik, Richards, Colaiacovo, Upshall, Chistov and Alexeev combined raises of $5-8M in total and still run a healthy operation. No cap to worry about.

**The 34+ money is the release valve.** Belfour ($6.50M), Mogilny ($5.50M), Svehla ($3.60M), Roberts ($2.70M) together cost $18.30M and carry $0.90M in combined point output beyond Mogilny. Mogilny and Belfour are already flagged as deadline trades. Svehla (18 GP, scratched) and Roberts (lined but 38 with POTE 52) are the natural cuts at season's end. Shedding those four frees the cash to pay the young core without touching the Sundin and Afinogenov long deals.

**Draft capital is ammunition, not a liability.** One first (from DET), one second, one third, one fourth. The DET first plus Holden is earmarked for Jackman at the deadline. After that deal the club still owns its second and can use it for a young player if the toughness target falls through. This is adequate for a contender that should be buying, not selling, at the deadline.

**The three moves that protect three years:** Lock Nash, Gaborik, Richards and Colaiacovo on 5-6 year deals this summer at $1.10-1.50M (sign them at current salary before their value rises). Trade Mogilny and Belfour before the deadline for picks or young assets. Let Svehla and Roberts walk at season's end rather than re-signing 35- and 38-year-olds on one-year deals that create the same cluster next summer.

## Calendar

Are we buyers or sellers at the deadline, and what happens with seventeen contracts worth $28.60M that expire this summer? We are buyers — 24-6-0, six points clear of second, first in the East — and the summer is a re-signing job with three players to move before they walk.

**Jackman** (STL, 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.70M) is the deadline target. St. Louis at 7-16-2 has to shed. A second-round pick gets us a 23-year-old with three years of control who fixes the toughness gap the coach flagged — best on our roster is 70 — and he's not a rental.

**Sillinger** (PHX, FACE 96) or **Conroy** (CGY, FACE 93) fills the faceoff hole. Sundin at 86 is the only player who wins a draw at 80-plus; we lose three lines of draws every night. Both are second-round priced, neither worth the first-round pick Mogilny commands.

**Mogilny** (95 overall, $5.50M, two years left) is the sell. Scratched, producing 0.75 points a game, above 80 so the pick mechanic works. Move him before the deadline for a first or a high-potential young player; his value only falls after March.

**Belfour** (39, $6.50M, CONS 50) stays through the playoffs. He's the starter and we need him for a run. Then offer two years at $3.50–4.00M or let him walk. Do not trade the starter before the post-season.

## Summer

**Gaborik** (22, $1.10M), **Richards** (24, $1.00M), **Kaberle** (26, $1.90M), **Nash** (20, $1.20M): the four core locks. Five- or six-year deals the day free agency opens. Gaborik at 22 and $1.10M is the cheapest star in the league; his price only rises. Nash is the internal toughness answer at 85 TOUG, already dressed on line 3.

**Upshall** (21, $1.20M), **Eminger** (21, $1.20M), **Colaiacovo** (21, $1.10M), **Chistov** (21, $1.10M), **Alexeev** (22, $1.10M), **Holden** (26, $1.20M): six depth renewals on two- or three-year deals. Locking them all on five years recreates the cluster problem we are trying to solve. If Holden goes to St. Louis in the Jackman package, this drops to five.

**Svehla** (35, $3.60M) and **Roberts** (38, $2.70M): let go. Svehla at 35 on $3.60M is money that belongs to a 24-year-old. Roberts at 38 carries a toughness grade of 70 that is the best on our roster, which says the roster is past him. If either sits above 80 overall, move him at the deadline for a pick before he walks.

**Renberg** (32, $2.00M): one-year extension at a reduced rate or let go. Low priority.

**Tellqvist** (25, $0.80M) and **Aebischer** (26, $0.50M): the manual says check the goalies, and Belfour at 39 means we need a succession plan. Re-sign Tellqvist on two years at $0.80M. Aebischer at $0.50M is cheap insurance; keep one, not both.

**Smirnov** (20, $0.40M, POTE 70, zero games): release. The coach is right. He is not owed a roster spot.

## League scan

This phase asks who across the league fills Toronto's two playoff gaps — toughness and faceoffs — on clubs that have reason to sell, and what each would cost. Toronto are 24-6-0 and buying, not selling, at the deadline.

**Jackman (STL)** is still the best answer. 83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23 years old, $0.70M with three years left. He plays 31.9 minutes a night (990 in 31 GP), which tells you St. Louis lean on him heavily. STL are 8-17-2 with $56.63M payroll and only $12.00M profit; nine expiring contracts mean they are shedding. A second-round pick is the price. No one else at 80+ TOUG combines his age, contract and production this cheaply.

**Sillinger (PHX)** is the cleanest faceoff fix. 96 FACE, 88 ovr, 27 points in 26 games at 20.7 minutes a night, $1.80M expiring. PHX are 12-16-4 and out of the race with 14 expiring contracts. He does not help the toughness gap (71 TOUG), but he wins the draw on two lines and clears the coach's complaint about losing faceoffs on three. Second-round-priced rental.

**Conroy (CGY)** is the fallback if PHX won't move Sillinger. 93 FACE, 82 ovr, 36 points in 32 games at 19.9 minutes per night, $2.00M expiring. CGY are 9-20-2 with 10 expiring contracts and the second-worst record. Same profile as Sillinger: a draw-winning centre on a club that has to clear. 33 years old, same as Sillinger.

**Bell (CHI)** is the toughness option the GM should have in his back pocket if Jackman stalls. 80 ovr, 93 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 24 years old, $0.90M with two years left. CHI are 6-18-6, the worst record in the league. The problem is CHI are profitable at $22.88M, so they are not financially desperate, but 6-18-6 creates pressure to re-tool regardless. Bell is the cheaper, younger version of Jackman at a lower overall.

**Cammalleri (LA)** is the best young player available. 83 ovr, 98 POTE, 22 years old, $1.10M expiring. LA are 8-14-5 with 13 expiring contracts and $48.60M payroll. If LA are tearing down, a 22-year-old with 98 potential at $1.10M is the kind of asset you want on your roster in March. The DET first-round pick buys him. He does not fill either immediate gap, but he gives Toronto another high-potential young player to develop alongside the core.

**Abid (PIT)** is the budget depth target. 78 ovr, 95 POTE, 87 TOUG, 87 CHKG, 24 years old, $0.40M expiring. PIT are 9-14-5 with 14 expiring contracts. He is not a regular and not a starter, but at $0.40M with 95 potential and 87 toughness he is the kind of fourth-liner who fills a hole on an injury and gives the coach a body to dress. A third-round pick is the price.

**Komisarek (MTL)** rounds out the blue line if the GM wants a young defenceman with toughness. 80 ovr, 83 TOUG, 90 CHKG, 90 POTE, 22 years old, $1.10M expiring. MTL are 9-19-2 with 14 expiring contracts. He is not Jackman, but at 22 with 90 potential he is the kind of depth the manual says wins cups. A third or conditional second.

**Tkachuk (STL)** is the one player who fills both gaps at once: 94 FACE, 85 TOUG, 90 ovr. But he is 32, on $9.00M for three more years, and STL are unlikely to eat that salary or give up their top player cheaply. I would not chase him. The money is too much for a rental and too much for a 32-year-old on a contender's books alongside the 17 expiring deals already coming due.

**Kovalchuk (ATL)** is the biggest name available: 91 ovr, 21 years old, $1.10M expiring, ATL 7-18-2. But he is 21 with a franchise built around him. ATL may keep him even at 7-18-2 because he is the reason to rebuild. I would not open with a first-round offer; he is too expensive for the pick unless the GM is certain ATL will move him.

The plan is two deals and one optional depth move. Jackman for the second. Sillinger or Conroy for the DET first (or the DET first goes to Cammalleri if the GM values development over a faceoff rental). Abid or Komisarek for a third. Mogilny is the salary dump that frees the $5.50M if the GM needs room.

## Trade construction

This phase turns the league-scan shortlist into concrete proposals that both clubs would sign: who we give, who we get, what each side's books look like after, and why they say yes. Toronto are 24-6-0 and buying, so the priority is filling two gaps: toughness (nobody shows 80+ TOUG today) and faceoffs (Sundin at FACE 90 is the only 80+ draw winner, a 15-point cliff to Chlup at 75).

**Mogilny is the centrepiece of what we give.** He is 95 overall, 35 years old, $5.50M with two years left, producing 42 points in 28 games (1.50 points a game), and he is not lined. The trajectory phase says trade him. His value only falls after the deadline, and any club above 80 overall that we do not intend to re-sign can move for a pick. At 95 he still carries first-round weight even at 35. He is surplus, expensive, and his production is a selling point to a club that needs a top-six forward right now.

**Jackman is the toughness fix and Mogilny plus a second-round pick is the package.** Jackman is 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23 years old, $0.70M with three years left, playing 31.9 minutes a night for a team that is 8-17-2. St. Louis are financially pressed at $56.63M payroll with $12.00M profit and nine expiring contracts. Mogilny gives them a 95-ovr top-line scorer at 1.50 points a game who can anchor their second year of rebuild alongside the young core they are drafting. The $5.50M is a burden but their profit covers it. The second-rounder tips them toward rebuilding youth. If STL balk at the money, drop Mogilny and go second-round pick only, but acceptance on the pick alone is uncertain because Jackman is cheap, young, and a core piece they may keep.

**Sillinger is the faceoff fix and Holden plus the DET first is the package.** Sillinger is 88 overall, FACE 96, 27 points in 26 games, 27 years old, $1.80M expiring. Phoenix are 12-16-4 with 14 expiring contracts and want to clear his salary. Holden is $1.20M, 26, zero games played, not dressed, and not in the plan. Phoenix take on a cheap body and get a first-round pick from Detroit, which is premium currency for a club picking at the bottom third. We add $0.60M through the playoffs and then it's gone. The risk is that Phoenix want a young player instead of Holden; if so, swap Upshall (POTE 99, 12 points in 28 games, $1.20M) in and accept the development cost.

**Conroy is the fallback faceoff man.** He is 82 overall, FACE 93, 36 points in 32 games, 33, $2.00M expiring. Calgary are 9-20-2, the second-worst record, with 10 expiring contracts. They are more likely to move him than Phoenix are to move Sillinger. Same package: Holden plus the DET first. If the GM wants to preserve the DET first, a second-round pick plus Holden might close Conroy given Calgary's desperation, but that requires the second-round not already spent on Jackman.

**What I would not do:** Spend the DET first on Cammalleri (83 ovr, 98 POTE, 22, $1.10M expiring, LA 8-14-5). He is the best developmental asset on the board, but a 98-POTE 22-year-old does not win the draw in a second-round playoff series. The faceoff gap kills runs. If both the toughness and faceoff deals land and the GM still has appetite, Cammalleri is a summer free-agency target at $1.10M with no trade cost, not a deadline target for a first-round pick.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-17
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-17

Next game at FLA on Saturday 18 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question is whether our young players are getting the games they've earned, and it matters now because we're at 31 games in and the minutes a kid gets in December set the floor for what he's doing in March.

**Gaborik** is 42 points in 31 games at 18.9 minutes on the first line. POTE 90 is the lowest on this list, but the production is the best. He's earning every minute. No change.

**Nash** is 28 points in 31 games at 13.0 minutes on the third line. POTE 95. That's 0.90 points per game, a second-line rate on a third-line assignment. Earning his 100% share.

**Klesla** is 19 points in 31 games at 14.7 minutes. POTE 97. A solid rate for a third-line defenceman. Earning his share.

**Eminger** is 15 points in 30 games at 16.1 minutes on the second line. POTE 99. The minutes are right for where he sits. Earning his share.

**Chlup** is 17 points in 20 games at 11.8 minutes, and he's 18. POTE 95. That's 0.85 points per game for an 18-year-old. Morale at 82 is the only thing I'd watch, but it's not a problem yet.

**Koltsov** is 14 points in 17 games at 8.0 minutes on the fourth line. POTE 94. That's 0.82 points per game, a better rate per minute than anyone else on this list. He's producing above what 8.0 minutes should produce. He's earning more than he's getting.

**Spezza** is 14 points in 28 games at 8.6 minutes on the fourth line. POTE 99. He's producing at 0.50 points per game, which is fine, but 8.6 is the lowest MPG of any dressed young player. For a 99-POTE player at 21, that's a development risk. The production doesn't demand the third line yet, but the minutes should not be this low.

**Colaiacovo** is 8 points in 16 games at 17.5 minutes, 52% share. POTE 99. When he's dressed he's getting a real look, but he's sitting or being scratched half the time. The 17.5 minutes when he's in says the staff trusts him with the puck; the 52% share says they don't trust him with every game. That's a contradiction.

**Spacek** is 9 points in 14 games at 16.4 minutes, 45% share. POTE 91. Same pattern as Colaiacovo: a real look when dressed, a low share overall. He's 19 and getting 16.4 minutes when he's in, which is more than most players two years his senior get. The opportunity is there; the share is the question.

**Alexeev** is 19 points in 31 games at 10.3 minutes on the fourth line. POTE 94. 0.61 points per game is a good rate for a fourth-line assignment. Earning his 100% share.

**Chistov** is 7 points in 17 games at 10.1 minutes, 55% share. POTE 95. The minutes are right for where he sits. Not being wasted, not being pushed.

**Safronov** is 23, zero games, POTE 91, morale 100. I've flagged this before and I'm flagging it again. A 91 scouting number at 23 with no games played is a decision being made by default. The GM needs to name him in or out of the plan.

**Upshall** is 21, now scratched, 12 points in 28 games at 13.6 minutes. POTE 99. 12 points in 28 games is 0.43 points per game, below the rate of every other dressed young forward on this list. The scratch is justified by the production. If he's still in the long-term plan at POTE 99, the scratch is a development risk; if he's not, it's the right call.

**Smirnov** is 19, zero games, scratched, POTE 70. The lowest scouting number on this list by a wide margin. No production, no minutes, no share. He is not owed a roster spot right now.

## Development trends

The question is who is moving in the right direction and who is not, because the next two weeks decide whether the current line structure carries into the new year or gets rebuilt.

**Chistov, Eminger, Upshall** are the three to watch. Chistov went 0.29 to 1.00 points a game while his minutes jumped from 9.5 to 12.7. Eminger went 0.35 to 1.00 and 15.0 to 20.0 minutes. Upshall 0.33 to 1.00, 13.4 to 15.0. All three are producing at a first-line rate on minutes still below what their rating should give them. The increase is already happening and I would not push it further this week, but these are the players the top six gets more comfortable around.

**Koltsov** is the one stalling. He was 1.10 points a game on 8.7 minutes before the window; now 0.43 on 7.0. Production down, minutes down, at 23. The minutes were already being pulled, which is correct, but 0.43 points a game in 7 games is below what a fourth-line winger should be. If this holds for another three games he is not the answer at left wing and the GM needs to know.

**Fischer** at 24 has gone from 0.63 to 0.14 points a game while his minutes went up from 20.8 to 22.3. That is not age. That is a player playing more and producing far less. I do not know whether it is hands or fit, but the numbers say he is not the D we thought he was at this stage.

**Sundin, Mogilny, Roberts** are all showing the same pattern: minutes up, points a game down. Sundin 1.46 to 1.00 at 20.6 minutes. Mogilny 1.62 to 0.75 at 18.5. Roberts 1.29 to 1.00 at 21.3. At 33, 35 and 38 respectively, the fade is arriving and the extra minutes are not producing the extra offence. I would hold Sundin at 17 or 18 and trim Roberts to 18, and let the minutes go to Klesla or Eminger.

**Safronov** still has zero games at 23. I raised this on the 15th and it has not moved. Either he plays this weekend or he does not, and the GM needs to say which.

**Spezza** at 21: points a game ticked from 0.43 to 0.71 but his minutes dropped from 9.1 to 7.0. He is getting less of the game while the team gets better. That is the opposite of what a 21-year-old centre should be doing and I want to know why.

## Morale watch

The room is fine. No one is in danger of a morale spiral, and no one is carrying minutes he cannot handle. One flag worth watching, one structural note.

**Spezza** dropped 4 points to 88 this week. He is on the fourth line at 8.6 minutes a night, 14 points in 28 games. His production is strong for those minutes, and per the GM's guidance I am not penalising him for being on L4. But 8.6 is under the 10-minute band I would expect for a player producing at his rate, and the drop is the only meaningful movement among dressed skaters. I am not pulling him up a line over one save's worth of movement. If he drops another 2 or 3 in the next couple of weeks and is still on L4 at under 9 minutes, that is when I would move him to the third line. For now: watch, do not act.

**Chlup** is the lowest dressed forward at 82, 11.8 minutes, 17 points in 20 games at 18. He is stable and producing well. No change. His minutes are appropriate for an 18-year-old on the third line, and the GM has told me not to treat production as a problem to fix by changing the line.

**Sundin** is at 88, 17.7 minutes, 42 points in 31 games at 33. He is under the 20-minute mark I would want for a top-line centre, but he is stable and the rate is fine. No change.

**Aebischer** sits at 80, the lowest on the roster, and has not moved. He is a scratched backup goalie with no ice time to give him. That number moves with results and the building, not with a lineup decision. If it drops below 80, that is the GM's to solve with the locker room or a win streak.

## Role composition

The question is whether each unit is built from players who suit it, and whether the roster holds enough of each role. It matters because FLA at 11-16 is a team we should beat without making changes, and if I am going to recommend a swap I need to be sure it is warranted.

**The lines are right as they stand.** L1 is the top scoring line (scoring 86/99, playmaking 84/99) with Sundin, Gaborik, Roberts and McCabe. L2 is the playmaking line (playmaking 82/95) with Spacek, Kaberle, Richards and Afinogenov. L3 is the speed line (speed 85/96) with Chlup, Colaiacovo, Klesla and Chistov. L4 is the special-teams line (speed 87/99) with Alexeev, Koltsov and Spezza. Each line has a clear identity and the players on it match that identity. I would not move anyone.

**The power plays split correctly.** P1 (Spacek, Sundin, Roberts, McCabe, Kaberle) is the safe PP, built to protect the net. P2 (Colaiacovo, Richards, Alexeev, Gaborik, Fischer) is the speed PP, led by Gaborik at 96 scoring and 99 playmaking. The two serve different purposes and the split works.

**The penalty kills are the one place I would push back on a criticism.** K1 (Roberts, Colaiacovo, Gaborik, Fischer) is a speed kill, anchored by Gaborik at 99 speed and Fischer at 91. K2 (McCabe, Kaberle, Richards, Chistov) is the checking kill, with Kaberle and McCabe doing the blocking. Gaborik on K1 looks like a waste of a 96 scorer, but his speed is the point. I would not pull him off it.

**The gaps are in the roster, not the arrangement.**

**Faceoffs.** Sundin at 86 is the only centre at 80 or above. Chlup is 75, Richards 72. We lose the draw on three of four lines every game, and our defencemen pick up coverage they should not face. No rearrangement of these players fixes that. The GM needs a centre at 80+.

**Finishing power.** Best toughness on the roster is 70, shared by Roberts and McCabe. Fischer is 69. No one can finish a check. Against a team that plays hard in the corners, we have no one who can make the play count. This is a roster addition, not a lineup fix.

**L4 stamina at 50/50** is a limitation I cannot fix with a lineup change. If the game is close late and these three are called on, they do not have the engine. It is what it is until the roster changes.

For Saturday at FLA: no change. The lineup is built for this game and FLA is not a team that requires a different one.

## Opponent matchup

The question this phase answers: does FLA force a change from the lines I'd run against anyone?

**Luongo** is the only thing that matters here. OVR 94, glove 99, save 95. He is not a goalie you outshoot into submission. FLA is 11-16 and their power play is 9-for-61, but Luongo keeps games within reach. That is a game-plan note, not a lineup one: shoot more, don't settle for the first chance.

**Nieuwendyk** at FACE 95 on their top line is a real faceoff problem against Sundin at 86. I have already flagged this as a roster gap, not a lineup fix. Swapping Richards (FACE 72) in front of him makes it worse, not better. The line stays.

**Jokinen** at 85 on their second line is a legitimate top-six forward. PUCK 88, DEKG 90. Our second line handles him. Richards at 84, Spacek at 74, Afinogenov at 83: that is a good line against a good line.

**Their bottom pair** is Van Ryn at 71 and Trnka at 70, with Ulanov and Laus at 68 on the fourth. That is a soft group. Our third and fourth lines have speed to exploit it in transition. No lineup change needed; just play to that.

**Belfour** starts. 91 OVR against a 94. That is a one-point gap, not a dilemma.

No change.
