# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-17

Toronto 23-6-0, 50 pts after 31 games.

## Role coverage

This phase answers which roles are thin or missing at 23-6-0 and which of those the coach can cover with who is already dressed, because the deadline buys should target only what he cannot. The gaps are two: toughness, and a second faceoff man. Everything else is covered, some of it aging.

**Toughness** is the missing role: the club has zero players the grades put at 80+, and the coach's report says the best dressed toughness is 72. That understates what is already on hand. **Nash**, 20, 80 overall, reads 85 TOUG and 80 CHKG today and is already dressed on line 3; **Tucker**, 29, 81 TOUG and 85 CHKG, sits not lined on $1.3M. Dressing Tucker gives the coach a real floor now, but neither man is a top-six finisher. That is the piece acquisition adds: **Jackman** (83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.7M) at a second-round price from a 7-16-2 St. Louis that must shed is the live buy, and he carries the role for years. **Bertuzzi** (95 overall, 89 TOUG, 29, expiring) covers toughness and scoring at once, but Vancouver at 14-8-2 may keep him and the price starts at Mogilny plus a first.

**Faceoffs** is the second real gap: **Sundin** at 90 is the only man at 80+, next is **Chlup** at 75 and he is 18. Three lines lose the draw every night, and this one is acquisition-only at the level wanted: **Sillinger** (FACE 96) or **Conroy** (93), each second-round priced, each a rental that plays behind Sundin while Chlup develops.

**Checking** is covered but aged at the top: **Roberts** 86 at 38, **Svehla** 83 at 35 and not lined, with **Fischer** 82 at 24 and **Upshall** 80 at 21 as the next pair, the latter two not lined. **Scoring**, **playmaking** and **speed** are the club's strengths: 13, 12 and 25 men at 80, and the core is young, **Gaborik** 92 at 22, **Richards** 85 at 24, **Spacek** 84 at 19. **Mogilny** at 94 but 35, not lined, 0.75 points a game, confirms building the top six without him. **Goal** is covered: **Aebischer** (84, 12-3, 2.80) and **Belfour** (91, 9-1, 2.57) are both playing; the only decision on Belfour at 39 on $6.5M expiring is summer's.

Decision: two acquisition targets, Jackman for toughness and one faceoff rental; every other covered role is a coaching choice, and dressing Tucker is the immediate internal move.

## Trajectory

Does this club age into a cliff, and is its money arranged for the next three summers? No to the first, and not yet to the second: the age curve is young and self-replacing, and the real cliff is the calendar, where 17 contracts expire together this summer for $28.6M.

**Gaborik** at 22 carries 42 points in 31 games, Nash at 20 has 28, Richards at 24 has 32, and Eminger at 21 with Spezza at 21 both hold top-four roles. Fourteen players are 23 or under; the 34-plus group is Belfour, Roberts, Mogilny and Svehla, all four expendable. This club ages in as that group leaves. It does not age into a cliff.

**Seventeen one-year deals**, $28.6M, come due in one summer, and they cover the entire young core the club must keep. Re-signing yearly only ratchets demands, and a core signed in one summer comes up again in one summer. The protection is staggered terms: Gaborik, Richards, Kaberle and Nash on 5-6 years now, the depth on 2-3.

**$13.7M** sits scratched in four veteran salaries: Mogilny $5.5M, Svehla $3.6M, Salo $2.6M, Renberg $2.0M. Payroll is $66.97M against $30.38M profit with no cap, so the club can afford an addition; what it cannot defend is paying four useful salaries for games nobody plays.

**Mogilny** is the move that protects twice. At 95 overall, 0.75 points a game, $5.5M with two years left and scratched, he is an above-80 expiring asset that prices as a first-round pick before the deadline and only less after it. Sell now; the pick replaces the one you spend.

**The Detroit pick** buys the next three seasons only if it buys a player with term, not a rental. Jackman, 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.7M from a 7-16-2 St. Louis that has to shed, is that buy.

**Belfour** stays through the playoffs, then walks or takes two years at $3.5-4M. $6.5M expiring at 39 with CONS 50 off a 10-game season is not a contract; Tellqvist at $0.8M and Aebischer at $0.5M are the pipeline that money should go to.

**Sundin** is the one veteran to mind: 33, $8.4M with five years left. It is justifiable while he is the only 80+ faceoff on the club, but years three to five are the risk once the draw problem is fixed.

## Calendar

The question this phase answers, with 51 games to go and the deadline some 74 days off: does a club at 23-6-0, 50 points and six clear of second place buy or sell in March, and what do the 17 expiring contracts cost. The answer: buy the one locked piece, sell the one fading asset, and sort the summer by locking five names.

## The deadline

**Jackman** is the deal I want made. St. Louis are 7-16-2 on a $56.6M payroll against $40.9M revenue, prestige 296; they shed, and he is 83 overall, 23, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, three years at $0.7M. That is the toughness buy and a top-four blueliner in one contract, and unlike a rental he is locked cheap. A second-round pick closes it. Every other piece I hold.

**Mogilny** is the one sell, and the coach gave the reason. He is 35 on $5.5M with two years left, scratched, producing 0.75 a game where he made 1.62; tonight he reads 85 on a 90 base. Above 80 he prices as a first-rounder and his value only falls from here. Selling clears his money and hands Chistov the longer look, Spezza the minutes. I would not do it unless the staff signs off that the top six holds without him.

**Sillinger and Conroy** fix the faceoff gap, but not for a pick. Sundin at 86 is the only centre who wins draws; Richards sits 72, Holden 66, Chistov 50, Spezza 51. Both rentals are 33, each priced at a second round, and we are first by six. A pick for two months of faceoffs is panic. Revisit only if the third line still loses draws at the deadline; otherwise plan it in summer.

**Bertuzzi** is the swing we take only if he signs. Vancouver reads 95, he is 29 on $2.6M expiring, and their 14-8-2 sits in the sell zone; he would cost our Detroit first and a player. A first for two months of a 95 is the rule against renting. Let Vancouver's February record decide, and insist on the re-sign before the pick moves.

## The summer

**Gaborik, Richards, Kaberle, Nash** are the locks and the standing rule is 5-6 years: Gaborik 22 at 95, Richards 24 at 84, Kaberle 26 at 81, Nash 20 at 80 tonight. Re-signing the same four every summer only ratchets what they ask. These go long first.

**Chistov, Upshall, Eminger, Colaiacovo, Alexeev, Smirnov** get 2-3 years, not five: Chistov 21 at 79, Upshall 21 at 76, Eminger 21 at 74, Colaiacovo 21 at 70, Alexeev 22 at 75, Smirnov 19 at 50. Locking the whole batch for five clusters their renewals again. Sign 2-3, extend when we can tell keeper from bust.

**Holden** stays on a cheap 2-3. He is 26 at 74 and $1.2M, the fourth-line centre, and the Ottawa package that once used his name died with their 11-11-3.

**Belfour** gets the goalie check first. He is 39 and 92 base on $6.5M expiring; offer two years at $3.5-4M reduced and find out before summer whether he takes it. **Aebischer** at 26 and $0.5M is the bargain backup either way and the starter if Belfour goes.

**Roberts and Svehla** earn two more years at reduced money and no more: Roberts 38 with 85 TOUG and 83 CHKG is the toughness floor when Nash sits, Svehla 35 at 85 base anchors the blueline. The older-player rule is about two.

**Renberg and Tellqvist** go. Renberg is 32 reading 76 tonight on $2.0M and the young wings are already dressed; Tellqvist is a third goalie at 73. Neither earns a renewal when the money can hold the five.

## League scan

Which clubs league-wide hold what our two gaps need, and which of them are willing to sell? The seller set comes off the standings and the money table: 17 clubs sit at 33 points or below, and within that group the ones with expiring deals and thin profit are the ones who will deal. The scan targets four classes on those clubs: 80+ toughness with checking, 90+ faceoff men, above-80 expiring assets priced at a pick, and 23-and-under high-potential depth worth owning through the summer.

**The seller set is crowded, so money separates it.** STL at 8-16-2 with 9 expiring deals and $13.4M profit is the urgent seller; that is why Jackman is the live toughness buy. MTL (14 expiring), FLA (18), LA (13) and PHX (14) have the same shape for the faceoff class — Sillinger in PHX and Conroy in CGY are the two named in the coverage phase. CGY at 9-19-2 and $13.7M profit is the poorest club in hockey and the most likely to shed anyone not signed long.

**Expiring assets price at a pick, so the seller's record matters more than his asset's age.** The Mogilny play — 95 overall, $5.5M, two years left, scratched — works against any club in the race; the above-80 expiring mechanic works against any club at all. The scan's third query finds who else across the bottom 12 sits at 80+ entering the last year of a deal, which is the class that converts to a pick without touching the roster.

**Young potential on losing clubs is the summer pipeline, not the deadline buy.** A 23-or-under player with POTE 85+ on a club at 33 points or worse is either a player they are rebuilding around (unavailable) or one a first-round pick can shake loose. The fourth query lists that class so the GM can see it before the deadline, even if Jackman and one faceoff rental are the only buys he makes now.

The four queries return the candidates; round two pulls ages, production and minutes on the shortlist.

## Trade construction

This phase settles what we actually trade for the two gaps, toughness and a second faceoff man, and what St. Louis, Calgary and any contender get in return that makes them say yes. Three moves, two buys and one sale: **Jackman** on a second-rounder, **Mogilny** out for a first-rounder before the deadline, and **Conroy** as the faceoff rental. All three give from surplus, which here is picks and an expiring veteran, and none touches the roles the coverage phase called thin.

**Jackman** is the one to do first. We give St. Louis our second-rounder, get Barret Jackman, 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, three years at $0.7M. Payroll adds $0.7M against $66.97M and $30.38M profit, and that salary is fixed for three summers, which is the point: this is the only buy with term, not a rental. St. Louis says yes because they sit 7-16-2 with nine expiring deals and a rebuild wants the pick. The weak link is that a 23-year-old on $0.7M is exactly the asset a rebuilding club usually keeps, so acceptance is the uncertain part of this deal. It is still the one move that fixes the role for years.

**Mogilny** is the sale that funds the deadline. Sell Alexei Mogilny now: 95 overall at 35, $5.5M with two years left, scratched, 0.75 points a game. Any contender in the race gets an above-80 scorer for a first-rounder, and his value only falls after the deadline. We shed $5.5M of the $13.7M that sits scratched in four veteran salaries, and the return first replaces the pick we spend on Jackman. It also closes the Coach's argument not to build a top six around a 35-year-old producing at half a point a game.

**Conroy** third, and only if the money holds. We give a second-rounder and get Craig Conroy, FACE 93, from Calgary at 9-19-2 with $13.7M profit, the poorest club in hockey and the most likely to shed anyone not signed long. Sillinger at FACE 96 is the alternative if Calgary prices higher. Either is a rental behind Sundin, turning three sub-80 draws a night into two while Chlup develops at 18; it costs only the term we were going to spend anyway. A last-place club cashing in a player who is not in its future is the cleanest seller on the board.

**If none land:** dress Tucker tomorrow, 92 CHKG and 88 TOUG at $1.3M, and that is the internal toughness floor. Live with Sundin alone on draws, keep the picks, and let Chlup at FACE 75 turn the faceoff problem into a development curve rather than a rental. A 23-6-0 club with $30.38M profit does not have to force a deal before the deadline, and that is a real answer, not a consolation.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-15
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-15

Next game at ATL on Thursday 16 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question is whether 30 games in each young player is getting the share he has earned — because at this point in the season the minutes are the roster, and a kid buried or parked is a decision that settles without anyone making it deliberately. Most of this group is being handled right. Four calls stand out, and two of them are the kind nobody notices.

**Spezza** is the one under-shared. 99 potential, 14 points in 27 games, and 8.9 minutes a night on the fourth line, with his morale (88) the second-lowest on the sheet. That production off a bottom-six share is exactly the "kid earns more than his slot" case the GM wants flagged, not graded. He is dressed nearly every night but buried; he has earned third-line minutes and the only thing standing between him and them is the centre squeeze that already has Chlup on L3. He should get a bigger share of this game, not the 19-year-old ahead of him.

**Smirnov** is the case I looked for and found the opposite. He sits at zero games, and the reflex is "wasted high-potential player." But his scouting number is 70, the floor of this whole group, and the three LWs ahead of him — Nash 28 points, Koltsov 14 in 16, Chistov 7 — are all producing. Zero games is correct for a 70-potential kid who would displace someone who scores. He is not owed a spot for being 19. No change.

**Safronov** is the one I cannot let pass quietly. 23 years old, 91 potential, and zero games all season — he is not fighting for a game, he is entirely outside the plan. That may be the right call behind Klesla, Eminger and Colaiacovo, but it is a decision being made by default, and at 23 with zero games the window closes fast. Decide deliberately whether he is in it or gone; do not let the season answer for you.

**Chlup** is getting his games — 11.6 a night on L3 and 17 points in 19 — so there is no development shortage. His 82 morale is the lowest on the roster, which is the team's record and his minutes talking, not a share problem, and I would not touch the games he has earned. **Spacek** (15.6 mpg on L2 at 19, morale 95), **Colaiacovo** (17.7 a night when he dresses), **Nash**, **Klesla**, **Eminger**, **Gaborik** (18.7 mpg and 41 points, the model for this), **Alexeev** and **Koltsov** are all dressed and getting real shares with high morale. **Upshall** is at 93% of games, so a scratch tonight is rotation, not neglect. **Chistov** backs up Nash and earns his rotation. None of those need touching.

## Development trends

Who is moving over the fortnight to December 15th, and does it change how I use anyone at Atlanta on Thursday. No grade on the card moved in this window, so every read below is production and minutes, and the windows are short: most of these kids have 2 to 6 games behind the second number.

**Chlup** is the loudest riser. At 18 he has gone from 0.62 points a game to 1.50, and his minutes have climbed from 11.0 to 13.0. Nine points in the six games since the first save, from a teenager, is a run you feed.

**Nash** has done the same on the wing, 0.83 to 1.33 points a game on 13.2 minutes. **Eminger** is the one already being paid for it: a defenceman from 0.35 to 1.17 points a game, minutes 15.0 to 20.2. He took the top-four workload and kept producing.

**Chistov** reads 1.50 points a game, but that is 3 points in 2 games, thin enough that I will not rebuild a line on it. **Klesla** at 1.17 is the same 6-game window as Eminger, more durable evidence.

**Spezza** is the one I would change. He is at 0.83 points a game on 8.2 minutes, the thinnest workload of anyone producing on this roster, and his minutes fell from 9.1. He is making his case on the shifts he gets.

**Koltsov** went the other way: 1.10 points a game down to 0.50, minutes 8.7 to 8.2. Six games at 23, and the scoresheet stopped arguing for him. **Spacek** held his rate, 0.55 to 0.50, on four fewer minutes a night, 16.0 to 13.5, so his usage dropped without his game falling off.

**Mogilny** is the veteran to plan around, and this confirms it: 1.62 points a game to 0.75 while his minutes went up, 16.9 to 18.5. More of the game is producing less. **Sundin** is at 1.46 to 1.00 on 19.7 minutes, still the first-line engine. **Roberts** at 38 is holding, 1.29 to 1.17 on 20.7 minutes.

## Morale watch

Morale against minutes the day before Atlanta, because one man's number is moving and his usage is the reason. The rest of the room is quiet: every dressed skater sits at 82 or better, most at 88 and above.

**Spezza** has lost 4 points in 11 days to 88 while playing 8.9 minutes a night on the fourth line. He has 14 points in 27 games, better than a half-point a game on fourth-line shifts. That is a player getting less of the game than his calibre expects, and it is the only usage problem on the sheet. I would give the fourth line more of the game rather than break a working top six in mid-December. Alexeev has 19 points in 30 games at 10.6 minutes and Koltsov 14 in 16 at 8.5; that unit has earned the extra shifts. A shift change will not reach his full 17-minute band from the fourth line, so if he keeps sliding I will move him up a line and wear the chemistry cost then.

**Richards** is down 3 to 92, but he is playing 16.9 minutes a night, which is the rate a top-six centre should get. His dip follows the results, not his usage.

**Aebischer** sits at 80, the floor of the room, across 16 games in goal. A goalie's workload is not a line-change lever and he already carries the larger share of the starts. His number moves with the results and the locker room, and that is the GM's to fix, not mine.

## Role composition

This phase asks whether each unit is built from men who suit it, and whether the roster holds enough of each role at all — and it matters now because our real problems are inventory gaps we cannot arrange around, not mis-assigned players.

**L1** is the one fully-formed unit on the club: Sundin's 88 faceoffs is our only 80+ draw man, McCabe and Fischer at 83 checking give it a shutdown core, and Gaborik's 98 scoring carries the offence. Properly built; leave it.

**L2** cannot check — 66 unit mean, and the only 80+ checkers we dress (McCabe, Fischer, Roberts) already sit on L1 and both kills, so there is no spare checker to move in even if I wanted to. This is a scoring unit with no shutdown partner beside it. That is a depth gap, not a mistake in who I assigned where.

**L4** fails as a checking line on both counts: checking 57 with nobody above Alexeev's 65, faceoffs 54 across the board. But Koltsov is producing at 99 speed and 89 playmaking, and per your standing call we grow these kids on their minutes rather than bench them for a checker. This is the accepted cost of the development line, not something I fix tonight.

**Power play** is balanced — a shooter on each unit, Sundin's 90 to P1 and Gaborik's 98 to P2 — and I have no production read on either unit to justify reordering men I cannot see. Leave both.

**Decision on composition: no change.** There is no rearrangement that fixes what ails us; the ails are inventory, and the smaller tool — share of the game — is the only move available, and even that is not called for tonight.

**Faceoffs** climb to Sundin 88 and drop off a cliff: Chlup 77, Richards 74, then 54s on L4, so three lines lose the draw every night. **Checking and toughness** give us three dressed 80+ checkers (McCabe, Fischer, Roberts, with Tucker 80 scratched) and a best toughness of 72 — one shutdown unit and no one who can finish a check. Both are roster gaps, already on record, and the lineup cannot fix either.

## Opponent matchup

The question this phase answers is whether Atlanta's look forces any change to how we play Thursday, and it does not — this is a mismatch so complete that the right call is to run the same group that has won ten straight and changed nothing.

**Atlanta** is 5-18-2, 102 goals for against 129 against, and 4.80 goals against per game, worst in this league by the look. Their power play is 9 for 66, 13.6 percent, so there is no special-teams concern to plan around. They beat nobody and give up nearly five a night; we scored 7 against them the one time we met. Nothing they ice asks us to adjust.

**Their threat** is two players, Kovalchuk (84) and Heatley (82). Kovalchuk carries SHPW 95, ACCU 85, DEKG 88 and plays the first line with Savard (FACE 81, their one draw winner). But there is no supporting cast behind that pair — the second, third and fourth lines are OVR 61–74 with nobody who finishes. Mark that first line, get our top pair against them, and the rest of their roster does not score.

**Our side** is healthy and sharp: Sundin (88) and McCabe (83) are back and fit, and Gaborik is a 97. We are 23-5, scoring 7.00 per game. Starting Belfour (93) is the call — this is exactly the road game you want your starter taking, and nothing Atlanta does argues for rotating Tellqvist in. That would be a workload or morale decision, and this phase is about the opponent; the opponent gives no reason.

No change before this puck drop. Reason class is matchup, and the reason there is no change is that the matchup creates no problem.

# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-15

Toronto 23-5-0, 50 pts after 30 games.

## Role coverage

Which roles can this club supply itself and which must be bought, with three-quarters of the schedule still ahead and the deadline set: at 23-5-0 the roster is good enough to plan acquisitions around its real holes. Coverage is strong at the top and the bottom of the sheet; the two roles with no internal answer are toughness and a second draw man.

**Scoring, playmaking, speed, clutch, stamina** are all covered and, more to the point, covered young: Gaborik 92 (22), Afinogenov 90 with 96 speed (25), Richards 85 (24), Spacek 84 (19). The only age in the attack is Mogilny 94 (35, not lined, fading at 1.62 to 0.75 points a game). The next three seasons of offence are already on the roster.

**Toughness** is the one missing role, and aged wrong: zero players at 80+, the top is Roberts 73 at 38. The only bodies who close that gap are Chara (92 TOUG, 27) and Bertuzzi (89 TOUG, 29). Tucker (29, not lined, 3 GP) is the internal floor, not a fix — dressing him nightly is the band-aid, and the slate gets a real answer only from one of the two targets.

**Faceoffs** is the thin role. Sundin 90 (33) is the only centre above 72 on the draw; the fourth line sits at 52/52. Chlup 75 (18) and Holden 71 (26, not lined) can take one line's draws, not three. Sillinger 96 and Conroy 93, each a second-round-priced rental, are the only way two lines win draws this year.

**Checking** is covered in numbers but not in the lineup — six at 80+, and three of them sit: Svehla 83 (35), Tucker 83 (29), Upshall 80 (21). The coach can fix that role tonight by dressing them; McCabe 86 (29) and Fischer 82 (24) carry it forward.

**Goaltending** is covered now — Belfour .907, Aebischer .890 — but Belfour is 39 and his $6.5M expires. That is a summer decision around Aebischer (26), not a deadline one.

Two targets carry into the deadline: one toughness (Chara first, Bertuzzi if Vancouver sell) and one draw man (Sillinger or Conroy). Everything else the coach fixes by using who he has, and the young core keeps this club from aging out except at the very top of the depth chart.

## Trajectory

Is this club aging into a cliff and is the money arranged sensibly? It is not the age curve that threatens the next three seasons — 14 of 32 players are 23 or under — it is the summer, with 17 contracts ($28.60M) expiring at once and a quarter of the payroll riding on four men 34 or older.

The curve is sound, even good. Fourteen under 24, eleven in their prime, and the potential carriers are already dressing nightly: **Gaborik** (22, 41 points in 30, $1.10M), **Nash** (20, 28 points), **Richards** (24, 31), **Klesla** (22, 19), **Alexeev** (22, 19). That is the manual's shape — a skein of young talent with 3-4 playing every night — so the thinness is not youth, it is the top.

The top is the problem. **Mogilny** (35, $5.50M, two years left) is scratched and fading — production 1.62 to 0.75 while his minutes went up — yet he still prices at 95 overall. **Svehla** (35, $3.60M) is scratched. **Roberts** (38, $2.70M) and **Belfour** (39, $6.50M) are both expiring, and Belfour is the only one of the four earning his keep in net. Together that is $18.30M, 27% of payroll, half of it on two men who never dress.

**Sundin** is the single long-term risk: 33 years old, $8.40M for five years — the only contract past four years on the sheet. You keep him, he is the draw (86 FACE, 41 points), but the years three-to-five of that deal are the one aging bet that can actually hurt.

The summer is the real bill. Seventeen players come due at $28.60M, and it splits almost exactly: about $11.9M is the young core (Gaborik, Richards, Kaberle, Eminger, Nash, Upshall, Colaiacovo, Alexeev, Chistov, Spacek) that you must keep and that will cost more than their current entry salaries; about $16.5M is vets (Belfour, Svehla, Roberts, Renberg, Holden) you will not re-sign. Profit is $29.57M, so there is room — the question is not money, it is not paying the vets twice.

Three moves protect the next three seasons. Lock the young core to 5-6 year deals the moment the season ends, before yearly re-signing ratchets Gaborik, Richards and Kaberle (their current deals total $4.00M combined). Trade the expiring vets at the deadline for whatever the market gives — Mogilny first, because 95 overall still prices him as an above-80 expiring asset, then Svehla and Roberts — rather than watch $16.5M walk for nothing. And spend the Detroit first on the deadline need (Chara at $1.7M, else Jackman at $0.7M on the second) while keeping Toronto's own first, so the draft hedge survives the deadline.

## Calendar

We are buyers — 50 points, six clear of New York, 52 games left — and the deadline plan is three need-buys, with the summer shaped by renewing the young core instead of the vets.

**Jackman** is the buy that matters most. The club's top toughness is Roberts at 70, and Jackman (STL) brings 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG at 23 with three years of control on $0.7M. That is the buy the manual prefers: a young player with potential, not a rental, for a second-round pick. The Chara alternative is dead — Ottawa sits 8th at 31 points, inside the race, so the Detroit-first package does not land.

**Sillinger or Conroy** is the faceoff fix. Sundin at 86 is the only centre above 72 on the draw and the fourth line sits at 52/52, so the three lines below Sundin lose the dot every game. Sillinger (PHX) is at FACE 96, Conroy (CGY) at 93, both second-round rentals. Take one.

**Bertuzzi** is the swing. He is the best player available at 95 ovr, 89 TOUG, 29, on an expiring $2.6M, and Mogilny plus the Detroit first is the package — the first is freed now that Chara is off. Mogilny is fading, 1.62 to 0.75 points a game while his minutes rose 16.9 to 18.5, so the top-six slot is open. Vancouver at 14-8-2 may keep him; if he lands he also closes half the toughness gap. Treat it as a no if it is not cheap.

The summer is a renewal of the core. **Gaborik** (22, $1.10M), **Richards** (24, $1.00M) and **Kaberle** (26, $1.90M) get 5-6 year deals — renewing them year to year only ratchets their demands.

**Eminger, Nash, Upshall, Colaiacovo, Chistov, Alexeev and Smirnov**, all on $0.4-1.2M and all expiring the same summer, get 2-3 years. That waits out the prospect-versus-bust call and staggers the next renewal so the whole core does not cluster again.

The crease is the one position where every goalie expires at once. **Belfour** at 39 and $6.50M stays through the run, then takes a reduced two-year offer at $3.5-4M or is moved as an above-80 asset for a pick.

**Tellqvist** (25, $0.80M) and **Aebischer** (26, $0.50M) are both too cheap to let go without choosing — renew one on 2-3 years as the future behind Belfour.

**Svehla** (35, $3.60M), **Roberts** (38, $2.70M) and **Renberg** (32, $2.00M) walk. Roberts' 70 is the ceiling on the toughness fix, not the fix; Jackman replaces it at 90. Svehla is the heaviest non-goalie deal on the list at a position the young blueliners cover.

**Holden** (26, $1.20M) is the sweetener if a deal still needs one; otherwise he renews 2-3 at that price.

## League scan

The deadline board is set by two gaps and one risk: toughness and a second draw man must be bought, and Mogilny's expiring 95 must be sold. The league table confirms the seller set. Ottawa sit 11-10-3 with 11 expiring deals and $25.32M profit; Vancouver are 15-9-3 (.617) with Bertuzzi's $2.6M expiring and only $34.94M payroll, so they can keep him or sell him; Phoenix (11-15-4, 14 expiring) and Calgary (9-17-2, 10 expiring) are both quarter-season rentals markets at the second-round price. Detroit's first round pick buys the top of this board, Toronto's own first stays home.

**Chara** remains the cleanest toughness target: 84 overall, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27 years old, $1.7M with one year left, on an Ottawa club that is 11-10-3 and a playoff longshot with 11 contracts expiring. Detroit's first plus Holden is the package, and it is the one move that closes the gap for years rather than months. The risk is Ottawa's three-point cushion over the playoff floor — if they string wins the deal dies.

**Bertuzzi** is the better player and the worse deal: 95 overall, 89 TOUG, 29, $2.6M expiring. Vancouver at 15-9-3 have an eleven-point window before sellers commit, and at 37 points they are priced like a contender. Mogilny plus a first is the only package that moves him, and it only works if Vancouver decides .617 is not the season. The price is the risk, not the player.

**Sillinger** is the draw rental: 96 FACE on a Phoenix club 11-15-4 with 14 expiring deals, second-round priced. He fixes two lines at once — the fourth line's 52/52 reads like a loss on every draw — and costs nothing that threatens the summer.

**Conroy** is the second draw option: 93 FACE, Calgary 9-17-2, 10 expiring, same second-round price. Cheaper than Sillinger on the sheet and the fallback if Phoenix over-asks.

**Jackman** is the toughness fallback if Chara dies: 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 23, $0.7M for three years, St. Louis 7-16-2, $56.63M payroll against $12.97M profit — the most financially pressed seller on the board. A second rounder buys six years of term. 

**Mogilny** (95 overall, 35, $5.50M, two years left, scratched and fading at 0.75 a game) is the expiring asset to sell — the above-80 mechanic means he prices as a first-round asset despite being a healthy scratch, and he should move before the deadline regardless of whether any of these deals land. Svehla and Roberts are the same class at lower prices.

Priority: Chara first, Sillinger second, Jackman when Chara dies, Bertuzzi only if Vancouver blinks. Conroy covers the draw if Phoenix won't sell.

## Trade construction

Three proposals, ranked, with money and the seller's record on each. The deadline needs are toughness and a second draw man, and the buyer's market is the league's rebuilding quarter: four sellers, all under .500, all shedding expiring deals. We pay with Detroit's first, our second, and a not-lined centre, never with the young core or the draft hedge.

**Chara** is the top move. We give Detroit's first and Holden (26, $1.20M, one year left, 81 overall, not lined) and get 84 overall, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG at 27 on $1.7M with one year left. Net payroll cost to us is $0.5M; Ottawa go from 11-10-3 with 11 expiring contracts and $25.32M profit, and Chara walks for nothing at summer otherwise, so a first plus a 26-year-old centre beats that. The risk is their three-point cushion over the playoff floor: if they string wins, he is not selling.

**Sillinger** is the second move, at the second-round price. We give the round-2 pick, get 96 FACE for the rest of the season from a Phoenix club 11-15-4 with 14 expiring deals, a pure rental seller. The money is small and off the summer books. Conroy (93 FACE, Calgary 9-17-2, 10 expiring) is the identical deal if Phoenix won't sell.

**Jackman** is the third, and in some ways the best value. The round-2 pick buys 83 overall, 90 TOUG, 23 years old, three years at $0.7M, the cheapest term on any board. St. Louis are 7-16-2 with $56.63M on the books against $12.97M profit, the most financially pressed seller in the league, and they shed three years of term for a pick. This is the Chara fallback, ready now.

If none land: dress Tucker (29, 92 CHKG, 88 TOUG, $1.3M, 3 GP) every night as the toughness floor, take draws with Sundin and Chlup (75 FACE) and accept losing the other lines until summer, keep Detroit's first for the draft, and move Mogilny (95 overall, $5.50M, two years left, a healthy scratch at 0.75 a game) anyway, since the above-80 expiring mechanic still prices him as a first-round asset regardless of which deals land. Bertuzzi is the swing only if both toughness targets die and Vancouver (15-9-3, $34.94M, $2.6M expiring) decides .617 is not the season; Mogilny plus a first is the only package, and the price is the risk, not the player.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-13
markdown:
# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-13

Toronto 22-5-0, 48 pts after 29 games.

## Role coverage

Are we covered at every role? Scoring, playmaking, speed, checking, clutch, stamina and goaltending are covered; the two true gaps are toughness, where we have zero players at 80 and our top is 73, and faceoffs, where Sundin 90 is our only man above 80 and the fourth line sits at 52/52. The scoring top is also aging underneath us.

**Toughness** is missing and only an acquisition fixes it. The best on the club is Roberts at 73 and he is 38; McCabe 73 is the other way, and the four usable checkers all live on L1 or the penalty kill. The coach can dress Tucker (83 CHKG, 70 TOUG, $1.3M) as a floor, but 70 is not 80. Chara (92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27, $1.7M expiring) is the cleanest deadline answer; Jackman (90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, $0.7M for three years) is the cheaper one that stays. Either is the acquisition this roster lacks.

**Faceoffs** behind Sundin is thin-to-missing. Chlup 75 at 18 and Roberts 75 at 38 are the next best; neither is a draw on a checking line, and the fourth line loses every one. Sillinger (96 FACE) and Conroy (93 FACE) are each second-round rentals that fix the two lower lines without touching the Detroit first. This is a buy-only gap at 80+.

**Mogilny** (94 ovr, 35, not lined) is the aging piece the coach flagged and I agree: his scoring is covered by Gaborik 92 and Sundin 92 for the years we need, so the first-round-plus-Mogilny package for Bertuzzi is the right way to cash him in. A 35-year-old not in any unit is a 94 overall on the bench.

**Roberts** (38, 98 durability, 86 CHKG, 73 TOUG) covers checking but not toughness and is a one-year piece; the moment Chara or Jackman lands, he becomes a 5-6 veteran on the third line, which is exactly the target shape. **Tucker** (29, 92 CHKG, 88 TOUG, $1.3M) is the internal floor: dressing him nightly costs nothing and gets a man who finishes a check, but he is a stopgap, not the fix. **Chlup** (18, faceoff 75, 0.62→1.40 this window) should keep growing his draws on the lower lines; he is the long-term faceoff hope behind Sundin, not the deadline answer.

## Trajectory

The question is whether this club ages into a cliff and whether its money is arranged for the next three seasons, not tonight. The answer is no cliff and mostly yes: 14 of 32 players are 23 or under, the four 34-plus players are three scratches and one fading winger, and the heavy money expires this summer. The risk is the summer itself, 17 contracts worth $28.60M, and the order they are renewed in.

**The age curve** is the healthy part. 14 players are 23 or under, and the production sits on them: Gaborik 22 with 39 points, Richards 24 with 30, Nash 20 with 26, Alexeev 22 with 19, all under $1.4M. The four 34-plus players, Belfour 39, Roberts 38, Mogilny 35, Svehla 35, carry three scratches between them. This is the manual's shape, many young with potential and a few veterans, and the veterans are the ones who disappear.

**The money** is split the smart way. $32.2M sits on six players: Sundin $8.4M, Belfour $6.5M, Mogilny $5.5M, Afinogenov $4.5M, Fischer $3.7M, Svehla $3.6M. Svehla has 14 points in 18 games and is scratched, dead money that clears on its own. The five best young producers cost $5.3M together. The arrangement works because the expensive part expires.

**Mogilny** is the one contract that outlives its player. 35, $5.50M for two more years, and his scoring fell from 1.62 to 0.75 points a game while his minutes rose 16.9 to 18.5. At 42 points today he still reads as a scorer to the league. Sell him at the deadline, as the ballast in the Bertuzzi package or for a pick alone, before the second year lands on a declining player.

**Sundin** is not a problem. 33, $8.4M on five years, 40 points in 29 games, the club's only draw above 72 at 86. That is a star on a long deal, the anchor to build around.

**The 17-expiring summer** is the real test. $28.60M comes off the book, and the veterans clearing, Belfour $6.5M, Mogilny $5.5M, Svehla $3.6M, Roberts $2.7M, Renberg $2.0M, is $20.3M of it, so the young core's raises are pre-funded. The order matters: Gaborik, Richards and Kaberle on 5-6 years first, the second tier on shorter terms so they do not all mature in the same summer.

**Belfour** is the one actual age cliff, a year out. 39, $6.5M for 10 games, backups Tellqvist 25 and Aebischer 26. Decide before summer: two years at $3.5-4M as a bridge, or trade him for the above-80-expiring pick and hand the net to the kids.

**The draft capital** is two firsts, Toronto's own and Detroit's. That is the ammunition for the toughness the coach says the club lacks, Roberts at 70 the best on the roster. Spend one on a young piece with potential, Chara 27 or Jackman 23, not a rental.

**Profit** clears: $30.38M on revenue $60.30M with no cap, so the club can add after the renewals. The constraint here is never money; it is not wasting the two firsts or the expiring veterans on the wrong deadline.

## Calendar

Are we buyers or sellers, and how do the two dates spend? We are first in the East at 22-5-0, 9 points clear of NYR with 53 games left — we buy at the deadline, and the summer is the real work: 17 contracts expire, and 9 of them are young players we want.

**Chara** (84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27, $1.7M) is the deadline's clean buy, Detroit's first plus Holden. The risk is real: Ottawa sit eighth at 29 pts and are 6-3-1 in their last 10 with 4.00 GF/GA — if they hold the playoff race the deal dies, and the fallback stays Jackman (83 ovr) at a second-round price.

**Sillinger or Conroy** fixes the faceoff gap the Coach flags. Only Sundin (FACE 86) and Chlup (75) are above 72 on the draw, and the fourth line sits at 52/52; Sillinger (FACE 96) or Conroy (93) at a second-rounder turns three losing draws a game into three won ones.

**Gaborik** (95 ovr, $1.1M) gets 5–6 years at whatever number it takes now. Locking him yearly only ratchets his demands, and he is the franchise piece. Same for **Richards** (84 ovr, $1.0M, FACE 72, our second centre) and **Kaberle** (81, $1.9M): all three signed 5–6, this summer, not next.

**Eminger, Nash, Upshall, Chistov, Alexeev, Colaiacovo** get 5–6 year deals as a block. Six of the nine carry potential at or near 99 (Eminger, Upshall, Colaiacovo all 99; Nash and Chistov 95; Alexeev 94) and Nash is already 80 ovr at 20. They re-sign in the same window — the clustering trap the manual warns about — but at $1.1M wage level the bill is affordable.

**Aebischer** (84 ovr, $0.5M) is the goalie answer. Lock him 2 years now; he is ready to own the net behind Belfour. **Belfour** (91, $6.5M) plays out this run, then gets the reduced two years at $3.5M, and if he balks Aebischer is the starter and we thank Belfour for the season.

**Roberts, Renberg, Svehla, Tellqvist, Smirnov** walk. Roberts is 38 at $2.7M, Renberg 32 at 76 ovr, Smirnov 19 at 50 ovr with 70 potential — the bust end. Svehla (82, $3.6M) is above the 80 line a contender pays a pick for, but we are that contender; keep him for the run, just do not extend.

## League scan

Whether the deadline has anything beyond the four names we already carry, and which clubs are the sellers, decides what we chase. The sellers are the bottom eight: ATL (18 pts), MIN (21), CGY (21), STL (22), CHI (22), LA (23), MTL (23) and PHI (25), with OTT (29) rebuilding on 11 expirings and PHX (28) and PIT (26) close behind. Everything we need sits inside them or at VAN, so round one asks the league-wide question four ways and comes back with a ranking.

**Chara** (84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27, $1.7M expiring) at OTT is the toughness fix, and OTT, 29 points and 11 expiring deals, is a club with no reason to keep him.

**Jackman** (83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, $0.7M for three years) at STL, 22 points, is the second-round toughness answer that stays past this spring.

**Sillinger** (96 FACE) at PHX, 28 points, and **Conroy** (93 FACE) at CGY, 21 points, each fix two of our three losing draw circles for a second-round rental.

**Bertuzzi** (95 ovr, 89 TOUG, 29, $2.6M expiring) at VAN, 15-9-3 and 37 points, is the scorer-and-toughness prize, but Vancouver sit in the West race and the sell window closes as they win; Mogilny plus the Detroit first is the price if it opens.

The wide queries run the same net over tougher checkers on the bottom eight, faceoff men above 88 anywhere, expiring 80-plus overalls on sellers with their production, and young producers on losers. Round two ranks what comes back and quotes each contract.

## Trade construction

The question is which of the four deadline names becomes a proposal we can actually push, and what each costs. Answer: three, ranked by how much they fix the club's one true gap, toughness, and every one buys from a seller with no reason to keep what we want.

**Chara** is first and priced. He is 84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27, $1.7M expiring, and Ottawa sit 29 points with 11 expiring deals. We give Detroit's first and Holden (26, 81 ovr, $1.2M, one year, no games), take on $1.7M that clears this summer. Ottawa get a first-round pick for a man who walks for nothing. This is the fix for the roster's worst gap, at the price already quoted.

**Jackman** is second, the value play that stays. 83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG, 23, $0.7M for three years at St. Louis, 22 points and bottom of the league. We give our second-round pick. He costs a third of Chara's money and is four years younger, and he is under contract past this spring. Chara is the stronger player for a 48-point year; Jackman is the one that pays into the next two seasons. Take Chara first, Jackman if that dies.

**Bertuzzi** is the swing, third. 95 ovr, 89 TOUG, 29, $2.6M expiring, and Vancouver at 15-9-3 and 37 points are still in the West race. We give Mogilny (35, 94 ovr, $5.5M with two years left, 42 points) and our own first. The money moves the right way, we shed $5.5M and take $2.6M. Mogilny is the one contract that outlives its player: his scoring fell from 1.62 to 0.75 a game while his minutes rose 16.9 to 18.5. Vancouver only says yes if they sell, and at .620 they may not. Take it if it opens; do not chase it.

**If none land**, the club is still 22-5-0 and the gap is not fatal. Dress Tucker (92 CHKG, 88 TOUG, 29, $1.3M) every night as the floor, keep Roberts on a checking line, keep both firsts, and let Chlup keep growing his draws. Keep the second for Sillinger (96 FACE) only if it survives the toughness deals; even then Chlup at 18 is the long answer on the dot.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-13
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-13

Next game vs NYR on Tuesday 14 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

Does the young core get the games it has earned? Mostly yes, and that is the honest answer: this club is already leaning on its kids, and no high-potential forward is being wasted. The two scratches, Smirnov and Safronov, are the only questions, and only one of them is a real one.

**Koltsov** is the strongest case for more. 13 points in 15 games is production at 8.6 minutes a night and he is only getting 52% of games. Per the GM's own measure, the scoresheet says he has outgrown the fourth line. Small intervention: give him more over the boards, not a linemate change.

**Spezza** reads the same way, softer. 13 points in 26 games at 9.0 minutes on the fourth line, and he shows the highest scouting number on the sheet. He is producing on his current role, not wasted, but 9.0 is at the bottom of the useful band and he has 90% of the games. He is being given the chance; he is just not being handed much to do with it. Fine to leave, worth remembering if a top-nine spot opens.

**Safronov** is the one genuine gap. 23 years old, a scouting number of 91, and zero games all season. He is not getting the chance to show anything. But the blue line is full of young men already getting theirs — Klesla 100%, Eminger 97%, Colaiacovo 48% at 17.9 a night — so this is a waiting list, not a snub. Worth a look when a defender misses time, not a roster change now.

**The rest need nothing.** Gaborik leads the club at 39 points on the first line, Nash 26, Alexeev 19 produced mostly from the fourth line, Chlup 15 in 18 as an 18-year-old, Klesla, Eminger and Colaiacovo all share the blue line fairly. Smirnov sits at zero games and zero points with the lowest scouting number on the sheet; that scratch is earned, not wasted.

One note that shapes all of it: with Sundin and McCabe both due back Tuesday, nobody young loses his spot because of this game. The minutes are where development happens here, and the only man being under-fed is Koltsov.

## Development trends

**The question is whether the kids' jumps are real and whether the veterans' drops are age, because that decides who earns more of the game down the stretch.** With no grade changes on any card this window, I am reading production against minutes, and the mover among the young forwards is Chlup.

**Chlup** went 0.62→1.40 points a game in five games and his minutes climbed with it, 11.0→13.0. At 18 he is our only young centre producing and the faceoff gap aside (86 FACE), he is the one kid I want more of. **Eminger** is the defender version of the same story: 0.35→1.20 and minutes up 15.0→20.4. What changed is he earned it, not that we handed it out.

**Nash** (0.83→1.20), **Upshall** (0.33→1.00, minutes 13.4→15.0) and **Klesla** (0.50→1.20) are all producing on steady or rising minutes. **Chistov** (0.29→1.00) is the one to watch — the production is there but only 11.0 minutes, so this is more streak than role yet.

**Spezza** is the stall to flag despite the 0.43→0.80 uptick: his minutes fell 9.1→8.4. The production is too thin to call development, and he is not getting the chance to prove it either. **Alexeev** at 0.62→0.80 on 8.8 minutes (down from 11.1) is actually efficient, not stalled.

**Mogilny** is the veteran who should change your plans. 1.62→0.75 while minutes went *up* 16.9→18.5 — a 35-year-old eating more game and producing half of it. **Sundin** (1.46→1.00, 16.9→18.6) and **Roberts** (1.29→1.00 on 19.8, up from 16.5) are cooler but still getting touches; Mogilny is spending his age the wrong way.

**My call:** keep feeding Chlup and Eminger, both are earning it, and start planning the top six around Mogilny's fading. He is not a scratch tonight — he is a warning for February.

## Morale watch

The question this phase answers: is anyone's morale slipping because I have him on the wrong minutes, with the Rangers coming in tomorrow? The answer is no — the room is in good shape and everyone who matters is steady. The lowest dressed man is Spezza at 88 and he is unchanged; the only sub-90 player on the whole sheet is Aebischer at 80, a scratched backup goalie, and no line change fixes that, so I name it and leave it to the GM.

**Spezza** is the only one I'd even glance at: 21, 88 morale, unchanged, 9.0 minutes a night on the fourth line with 13 points in 26 games. That is under the 10-minute band for a useful player, but he is a young centre developing on the fourth line, he is producing on those minutes, and his morale is not dropping. He is not complaining, so I do not touch him. If I moved him up it would be development, not morale — and his production says he is fine where he is.

**Chistov** (+2 to 92) and **Roberts/Richards** (+3 to 95) all rose; **Tellqvist** dipped one to 95 after his start. Nothing is sliding on minutes anyone controls. Everyone else of consequence — Sundin, Gaborik, Mogilny, Nash, the whole top four on the blue line — sits at 88 or better and steady.

The only thing I would flag as the GM's, not mine: **Aebischer** at 80 is the low man on the sheet, and he is a healthy scratch. His minutes are zero because he is not dressed; that is a roster call about whether we carry a third goalie, not a bench decision. And the 88s across the top line likely track the standings, not their minutes — they play 17–19 a night and hold 88–92, which is a results number, and the results are a GM problem nobody on the bench fixes.

## Role composition

This phase asks whether each unit has the right players on it, and whether the roster can fill the roles at all. The units are built about as well as this roster allows; the two things genuinely missing are roster gaps, not arrangement problems, and I already flagged both.

**L1** is the shutdown-and-score line and it is the right build. Sundin at 86 faceoffs is the only draw he wins with, Roberts at 80 checking and 70 toughness is the only enforcer, and Gaborik at 99 scoring is the finisher. It carries checking 77/88 and scoring 86/99. There is no better way to arrange our best checker, our best scorer and our only faceoff man together.

**L2** is a scoring line that is soft by design: checking 64/91, toughness 60/91. That is acceptable as long as it is not the matchup line. Spacek, Richards at 72 faceoffs and Afinogenov at 88 scoring are all built to attack, and Richards 94 clutch belongs in the offensive minutes.

**L4** is Alexeev, Koltsov and Spezza at checking 55/63, toughness 54/63 — it cannot check and 52/52 faceoffs says nobody wins a draw. But per the GM's standing order these three produce on their minutes and that is their role. Do not rebuild a line that is scoring; the grade sheet is what they grow out of.

**Gaborik** on K1 is the one wrong-looking piece: your only 99 scorer and 99 speed one-timer killing penalties because we are short a checker. That is not an arrangement error to fix by trading lines — the checking inventory behind the top unit is McCabe 81, Fischer 81, Roberts 80 and nobody else above 78, so the scorer eats the kill minutes because there is no one cheaper to send. It is a roster gap wearing an arrangement's clothes.

**Faceoffs** break at Chlup 75. Sundin 86 carries everything above that; Richards 72 and Roberts 73 are thirds, and the fourth-line centres sit at 52-53. We give away the draw on three lines a night. No lineup shuffle fixes that.

**Toughness** tops out at Roberts 70. Nothing on the roster finishes a check or punishes a physical team, and against a playoff opponent built to hit this is unsolvable from inside this room.

No unit needs rebuilding today. Both real holes are things for the GM's side of the desk.

## Opponent matchup

Does NYR's roster force an adjustment tonight? No. They are a good club — 44 points, a top line of **Lindros (89), Nedved (88) and Kovalev (90)** that can hurt anyone — but they give up 3.70 goals a game while we score 7.40, and they limp in having gone 3-3 in their last six after we've won ten straight. Nothing about this opponent requires breaking a working lineup.

**Lindros' line** is the only thing to respect, and we have the answer already on the ice. **Roberts (CHKG 83, TOUG 85)** and **Fischer (CHKG 87)** are the matchup and they are already on the first line and the top pair. No unit needs to be rebuilt to get a shutdown body on them.

**McCabe** is the one wrinkle, and it is injury-cover, not tactics. He is out tonight, back tomorrow. That leaves Fischer on the top pair with a fill-in at left defence, and of the dressed bodies none carries McCabe's CHKG 82 — which is what I would want on Lindros. Fischer has to anchor that pair alone tonight. One game, and the fix is him, so we ride it.

**Faceoffs** are the ugly known: they ice Lindros 88, Nedved 86 and Holik 95 on the dot, so we lose draws on at least two lines all night. That is the roster gap already on file, not something a lineup swap fixes, and it has not cost us through 22-5.

**Belfour (91)** starts and is the better goaltender on the night. Lines stay, net stays, McCabe's spot gets whoever fills it.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-11
markdown:
# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-11

Toronto 21-5-0, 46 pts after 28 games.

## Role coverage

The question this phase answers is whether the roster the coach can dress covers what a team needs, or whether a hole in the lineup is really a hole in the club. Toronto is 21-5-0, so scoring, playmaking, speed, clutch and stamina are not the issue — the issue is the two roles where the dressed club comes up short. Toughness is missing outright: zero players at 80+, with the best dressed option McCabe at 73. Checking is covered but its spine is aging — Roberts 86 at 38, Svehla 83 at 35 and not even lined. Faceoffs are one man deep: only Sundin at 90 sits above 80, and the next dressed option is Chlup at 75, an 18-year-old.

**Tucker** is the internal toughness answer and he costs nothing. He sits not lined with 3 games played; his 83 CHKG is already the third-best checking grade on the club, and the coach flagged him on Dec 7. Dressing him on L4 closes the toughest gap in the roster without a trade. He is the floor, not the fix — at 29 he is what we have, and my read is he is the band-aid until a real target lands, not the long-term answer.

**Chara** is the acquisition that fixes two roles at once and fixes the age problem underneath them. He is 84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG at 27, $1.7M with one year left — he replaces the aging checkers (Roberts 38, Svehla 35) with the same job at 27, and he is the only realistic way the checking corps survives past this season without a rebuild on the fly. The package of Detroit's first plus Holden is what I noted Dec 7, and the deal survives only while Ottawa stay out of the race.

**Faceoffs** are the gap the coach named that the roster cannot fix internally. Sundin 90 is the only man over 80; Richards 70 is the club's centre depth and loses draws at that grade. Chlup at 75 trends up but is 18 and not a this-season answer. No internal move changes the number — this is a genuine target, and it needs a name and a price before the deadline, because the pity is that a 21-5 club with one faceoff man gets exposed the first night a draw decides a playoff game.

**Roberts** is not a gap today but becomes one the day his legs go. 98 durability at 38 is exactly the grade that lies — he is at 22.0 mpg with production down to 0.50 pts/g, and that minutes load is the club spending a resource that ages. The coach flagged it; the redistribution is his to run, but the planning is mine, and the plan is that Chara at 27 is the replacement before Roberts is the hole.

## Trajectory

Is the age curve heading over a cliff and is the money arranged for what comes next? The curve is fine; the money is the cliff. Fourteen players are 23 or under, at least seven of them carry real potential, and four play nightly. The danger is not aging but clustering: 17 contracts worth $28.6M expire this summer, and $14.8M of that sits with the four players 34 and older.

**Gaborik, Richards, Kaberle** are the locks and the summer's cost anchor. Gaborik is 22, 38 points, $1.1M on a 1y deal. Richards is 24, 29 points, $1.0M, 1y. Kaberle is 26, plays 28 games, $1.9M, 1y. Sign all three now on 5-6 year deals, before the cluster. Every year they go unsigned is a year their price ratchets. These three are the first $6-8M of next summer's bill.

**The 34+ group** is $18.3M of payroll and three of the four expire now: Belfour 39 at $6.5M, Svehla 35 at $3.6M, Roberts 38 at $2.7M, Renberg 32 at $2.0M with Mogilny 35 at $5.5M on 2y. Letting Svehla, Renberg and Roberts walk this summer frees $8.3M for the young locks. Belfour is the one with value: the above-80 expiring mechanic says he can be turned into a pick, but the standing order is keep him through the playoffs, then two years reduced or a pick.

**The young expirings** are the rest of the $28.6M: Nash, Upshall, Eminger, Alexeev, Colaiacovo, Chistov, Spacek, Tellqvist, Aebischer, Smirnov. They sign this summer at 2-3 years, not long, because the danger of locking ten young players for five years is that they all come up again in one summer. The guide names that trap exactly; this roster is living it. Stagger the terms.

**Money room** is real but one-directional. Payroll is $66.97M against revenue of $60.30M with profit booked at $29.54M, so there is room to add a salary now. The summer is when the $28.6M lands. Spending power is now-before-July, and it should flow to the re-sign, not to a rental.

**Draft capital** is one premium chip: Detroit's first round. Your own second through fourth are depth ammo. The DET first should be spent only on a need that survives three seasons, the standing hole of a faceoff centre behind Sundin, who at 86 is the only one who wins draws, or a toughness target. A rental for a first is the one way to lose this summer twice.

## Calendar

As of Saturday 11 December 2004 we are buyers: 21-5-0, 46 points, first in the East four clear of NYR (42) with 54 games left and the deadline about 80 days out, which makes this the moment to fix the one real hole and plan a summer that locks the young core before seventeen contracts expire.

**The deadline.** Buy for the hole the Coach names: a centre who wins draws. Only Sundin stands at 86; everyone else is below. A first or second round pick is the guide's price, and we prefer a young player with potential over a rental. The toughness blueliner is secondary and internal.

**Chara** is the standing toughness target — 84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 27, $1.7M, one year left — but Ottawa sit 8th at 28 points, exactly on the playoff line, and the standing rule is that deal dies if they stay in the race. Detroit's first plus Holden stays ready; treat acceptance as lower confidence. If it fails, Tucker (29, 92 CHKG, 88 TOUG, $1.3M) is the floor, dressed nightly.

**Belfour** is the whole crease question. Keep him through the run, then offer two years at $3.5-4M against his $6.5M; if he refuses, Tellqvist (25, $0.8M) starts and Aebischer (26, $0.5M) backs him cheap.

**Roberts** is a let-go: 38, $2.7M, and the Coach has him at 0.50 pts/g on 22.0 minutes. Those minutes belong to Nash and Koltsov. **Svehla** at 35 and $3.6M is the trade-before-expiry candidate — if he clears 80 by March, move him for a pick rather than pay a 35-year-old into decline with Eminger (21) and Colaiacovo (21) behind him.

**Gaborik**, **Richards**, **Nash**, **Kaberle** are the four locks — 22, 24, 20, 26, at $1.1M, $1.0M, $1.2M, $1.9M. Sign all four on 5-6 years now; re-signing yearly only ratchets their demands. **The six young depth** — Upshall, Eminger, Colaiacovo, Chistov, Alexeev, Smirnov, all 19-22 — sign 2-3 years, staggered so the class never comes due in one summer, and extend the ones who prove it.

**Holden** (26, $1.2M) is the Chara chip; if the deal stalls he earns a short renewal only by producing in March. **Renberg** (32, $2.0M) gets a two-year keep if he is contributing at the deadline, otherwise he walks with Roberts.

## League scan

The question for the wide scan: which rostered players across the league, on clubs likely to sell, fill the two genuine holes on Toronto's dressed roster — a centre who wins draws behind Sundin and a toughness grade that currently maxes out at McCabe's 73 — and which losing clubs hold young, high-potential players and expiring veterans worth a pick. The race column sits at 46 points, so these are deadline questions, not summer questions.

**Faceoffs** — the coach named this gap and the coverage phase confirmed it: Sundin 90 is the only dressed centre over 80, Richards 70 loses draws behind him, Chlup 75 is 18. The scan targets every centre at FACE 80 or better league-wide, then filters by club record. The seller list from the trajectory sheet is deep — ATL, MIN, CHI, CGY, STL, MTL, LA at 23 or fewer points — and any of them holding a second faceoff man with a moveable contract is a target.

**Toughness** — zero Toronto players at TOUG 80+, so the bar is everyone at 82/85 or better in TOUG/CHKG who might move. Chara at OTT (92 TOUG, 93 CHKG, 84 ovr, 27, $1.7M, one year) is the known clean target, and OTT at 28 points with 11 expiring deals is still the ideal seller. The scan looks for a second name in that class so the Chara deal is not a hostage situation.

**The young, high-potential class** — the draft-class players (ids above the disc space) carry revised per-snapshot ratings, so they need their own query through `player_attribute_state.ratings`. The target is anyone 23 or under, POTE 85+, overall 76+, sitting on a club at 32 points or fewer — the Gaborik-on-a-bad-team prize that turns a pick into a 22-year-old core player.

**The expiring class** — seventeen of our own contracts expire this summer; the league has the same distribution. The scan pulls every player on his last year at overall 80+ from a club at 31 points or fewer, because that is the rental market where Detroit's first either buys three seasons of need or buys a mistake. The DET first only moves for a need that survives July.

## Trade construction

Which two or three trades actually get written, and why does the other club sign — record, money, the hole they are dumping. Toronto's two holes are toughness (best dressed option McCabe at 73) and a draw winner behind Sundin 90, and the seller list is deep enough that both have clean names. Ranked below; every package hews to the standing rule that the Detroit first only moves for a need with term, and everything else we give is expiring.

**Chara plus Todd White from Ottawa** is the one negotiation that closes both holes, at the cost of the chip. Chara is 84 ovr, 92 TOUG, 93 CHKG at 27, $1.7M with one year left — he replaces Roberts (38, 22.0 mpg, production down to 0.50 pts/g) with the same job nine years younger. White is 83 ovr, FACE 81, $0.9M expiring, and would be our second-best draw man by a mile. Ottawa sit 10-10-2 on 28 points with 11 expiring contracts; a rebuilding club trades expiring veterans for picks and young players, and White and Chara both walk or move anyway. The DET first plus Holden (26, 0 GP, expiring) plus one young defender clears it. The risk is the one that kills it: Ottawa at .500 can climb into the race, and the deal dies the day they do.

**Barret Jackman from St. Louis** is the value play underneath: the same need, term included, at a fraction of the price. He is 83 ovr, 90 TOUG, 91 CHKG at 23, on a $0.7M contract with three years left. St. Louis are 7-15-2 on 22 points, third-worst in the league; they sell everything, and a 23-year-old at $0.7M is exactly what a seller says yes to for a second-round pick. This is a toughness fix that outlives the deadline, costs our second and a young surplus forward (Upshall, 21, expiring), and leaves the DET first in the drawer. If Chara's deal dies, this is the answer, and it is cheaper than Chara's alone.

**Mike Sillinger from Phoenix** fills the faceoff hole as a pure rental, second-round price, DET first untouched. He is 88 ovr with FACE 96, the best draw grade in the entire pool, at 33 on a $1.8M expiring contract. Phoenix sit 10-14-4 on 26 points and are sellers; a 33-year-old expiring centre they will not re-sign is worth a second-round pick to them. The alternative if Phoenix holds out is Craig Conroy at Calgary — 82 ovr, FACE 93, $2.0M expiring, and Calgary at 9-17-1 are the worst club on the sheet. Either is a rental, which is why neither draws the first. The caution: Sillinger and Chara can be combined, but then you are paying a first for the toughness AND a second for the draw, and the summer bill you are protecting is already $28.6M.

Payroll is not the constraint: the club runs $66.97M against $60.3M revenue with $29.54M profit booked, and every player above except Jackman is expiring, so none of this worsens the summer cluster. If none land, dress Tucker (88 TOUG, 83 CHKG, $1.3M) every night as the toughness floor, and live one-deep on faceoffs behind Sundin — Richards 70 and Chlup 75 at 18 are not a this-season answer, so the draw gap carries to the deadline or the summer, not to a bad panic price.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07
markdown:
# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07

Toronto 19-5-0, 42 pts after 26 games.

## Role coverage

This phase asks whether Toronto have enough bodies at each role for the next three seasons, and which gaps the coach can plug internally versus which need a trade. The answer: scoring, speed, playmaking and clutch are covered in depth; checking is thin and aging; toughness is missing outright with zero players at 80+; and faceoff centres are a single-man show behind Sundin. Two of those three gaps cannot be fixed by shuffling lines.

**Toughness** is the structural hole. Nobody on 32 rostered skaters carries an 80 in the toughness grade. The best is Roberts at 73 (38 years old) and McCabe at 73 (29). Tucker, who the coach may want on the PK, sits at 70. Svehla is 69 at 35. This is not a line-assignment problem; the personnel do not exist. Every playoff series in this league has a physical test, and Toronto are built to fail it. Only an acquisition fixes this.

**Faceoff centres** are the second gap. Sundin 90 is the only centre above 80 in FACE. Richards is 70 at 24, which makes him a second playmaker, not a second centre who can hold the ice against top lines. Chlup is 75 at 18, a kid. Holden is 71 at 26 and not lined. The coach flagged this and he is right: behind Sundin there is no one whose draw win rate is a reason to dress him.

**Checking** at 6 players above 80 is thin but survivable for a year. McCabe 86 (29) and Fischer 82 (24) are in their prime. Upshall 80 (21) is a prospect. The problem is the other three: Roberts 86 at 38, Svehla 83 at 35, Tucker 83 at 29 and not lined. If Svehla and Roberts decline together, this drops to three. Tucker is the internal band-aid if the coach will dress him.

**Koltsov** is the clearest waste. Speed 92, age 23, 12 points in 11 games at 1.09 points per game, and the coach says he is being healthy scratched. The club has 25 players with speed above 80, which means there is no shortage of fast wings, but a 23-year-old producing a point a game who is not in the lineup is both a morale risk and a development stall. He needs to be dressed.

**Spacek** at playmaking 84, age 19, and not lined is the other development flag. The coach says he went from 16 minutes a game to scratched with no injury. If the club scratched a 19-year-old showing 84 playmaking, that needs a reason beyond a coach's preference. His stamina and durability numbers (79 durability) are not great, but he is 19.

**Goalies** are covered for this run. Belfour at 92/92 glove grades, 2.57 GAA, 0.907 SV% is still starting-calibre, but he is 39 on $6.50M expiring. Aebischer at 26, $0.50M, 3.00 GAA, 0.884 SV% is a real backup. Tellqvist is depth. No trade need here short-term; the summer question is Belfour, and that is already noted.

## Trajectory

**The trajectory question: can this club re-sign its own core, and does the 34+ payroll make the answer harder?** The answer is that the youth pipeline is deep enough to sustain three competitive seasons, but the summer 2005 cliff — 17 contracts, $28.6M walking simultaneously — is the entire dynasty challenge, and the four players aged 34+ eating $18.3M make re-signing the young core costlier than it needs to be.

**The age shape is not a cliff.** Fourteen players at 23 or under, eleven at 24-29, only three at 30-33, four at 34+. In five years, the 24-29 group becomes the 29-34 bridge and the youth fills in naturally. The thin 30-33 band is a one-season gap that fixes itself. The structural risk is not aging; it's the contract cliff.

**Gaborik** at $1.1M, 34 points in 26 games, 90 potential, one year left. He is the cheapest top-line winger in the league and the first player who must sign a 5-6 year deal this summer. Nash ($1.2M, 23 pts, 95 POTE, one year), Richards ($1.0M, 28 pts, 88 POTE, one year), Eminger ($1.2M, 11 pts, 99 POTE, one year) follow immediately. These four cost $4.5M combined today and will cost $12-16M on new deals. The $29.5M profit absorbs that comfortably.

**Kaberle** is the exception. At 26 with 75 potential and $1.9M, he is less a "lock up on potential" case than a "productive today, replaceable tomorrow" case. A 5-year deal is defensible at $2.5M but not urgent. Priority is below the four 95+ potential players.

**The 34+ group costs $18.3M for players in their last productive years.** Belfour ($6.5M, 39, 10 GP), Roberts ($2.7M, 38, 32 pts in 26), Svehla ($3.6M, 35, scratched), Mogilny ($5.5M, 35, 39 pts in 26). Mogilny is the hardest call: he has 2 years left so he cannot simply expire, and his production is genuinely good. But at 37 he'll be a $5.5M anchor with 55 potential and no market. The deadline is the window to move him while another club wants a playoff scorer.

**Belfour is the deadline asset.** $6.5M expiring, 39 years old, potential 50. The above-80 expiring mechanic works. Aebischer ($0.5M, 90 POTE, 26) is already the starter; Tellqvist ($0.8M, 91 POTE, 25) is the backup. Goalie coverage is solved at $1.3M. Use Belfour's contract for a first-round pick or a young defenceman.

**Draft capital is strong: two first-rounders (TOR's own and Detroit's), plus second, third, and fourth.** This is deadline ammunition. If the club buys at the trade deadline, the two firsts can acquire a top-4 centre or a second-line scoring winger without touching the youth core. If the club stands pat, they are summer picks that feed the pipeline.

**The move list, in order of consequence:**

## Calendar

**Are we buyers or sellers at the deadline, and what do we do with 17 expiring contracts this summer?** We buy. At 19-5-0, 42 points, first in the East with 8 of 15 making the playoffs, we are the clear contender. The deadline plan and the summer plan are one problem: lock the core, move the old money, plug the centre gap.

**Svehla, Roberts, Renberg.** Three veterans on expiring deals — 35 at $3.60M, 38 at $2.70M, 32 at $2.00M — that add up to $8.30M we should not carry into next season. Move all three before the deadline for picks. Any of them above 80 overall can be flipped for a draft pick using the expiring-asset mechanic. If they are below 80, find a club that needs a veteran blueliner or a left winger and take a late pick. Do not let them walk for nothing.

**Belfour** at 39 and $6.50M is the biggest single contract in the building. The read from the prior note stands: keep him through the playoffs, then offer two years at $3.5-4.0M or move him for a pick after the Cup run. At 39, a one-year re-signing next summer just re-creates this exact problem.

**Kaberle, Gaborik, Richards** are the three that cannot leave. Kaberle at 26 and $1.90M, Gaborik at 22 and $1.10M, Richards at 24 and $1.00M — all prime-age or near it, all cheap relative to their value. Each gets a 5-6 year deal the moment the season ends. Richards directly answers the coach's centre-gap flag: at 24 and $1.0M, he is the guy behind Sundin and he is about to walk.

**Nash** at 20 and $1.20M is the same story on a longer timeline. Lock him on a 4-5 year deal. The coach is already using him on the penalty kill, which means he is in the lineup.

**Eminger, Colaiacovo, Chistov, Upshall, Alexeev, Smirnov.** Six players aged 19-21 at $1.20M or less. These are depth pieces we should re-sign on 2-3 year deals, not 5-6. They are not proven enough for long term, but at those salaries the risk is minimal. Re-sign them cheap, develop them, and extend the ones who stick around year three.

**Holden** at 26 and $1.20M sits between the core and the depth group. He is the 2C we need behind Sundin if Richards stays at centre. Re-sign on 2-3 years. If we move him, we create the gap the coach is already complaining about.

**Tellqvist at 25 and $0.80M, Aebischer at 26 and $0.50M.** Both cheap, both young enough to develop. Re-sign both. The guide lost good goalies by forgetting. Aebischer at $500K is the best-value contract in the building.

**The deadline plan is two moves:** First, sign Richards to an extension so we are not trading from desperation later. Second, package Svehla or Roberts — whoever a contending club needs — for a pick and maybe a young prospect. We do not need to sell. We need to buy depth on the back end and clean house on the expiring money.

## League scan

**The question: who in this league fills Toronto's toughness and centre gaps, on a club that has a hockey reason to say yes?** The answer is that three players stand out — one is the best available asset in the entire league, and two of his peers sit on clubs that are mathematically rebuilding with expiring deals and no path to keeping them.

**Todd Bertuzzi** at VAN is the target. 95 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 29 years old, $2.6M, one year left. Vancouver are 14-8-2 with the lowest payroll in the league at $34.94M and $21.93M profit. They went zero rounds in the playoffs last year. A 95-overall player will demand $5-6M on his next deal; Vancouver probably won't go there. They trade him for a first-rounder and a rental rather than lose him for nothing in July. He fills the toughness gap AND gives a second line of scoring that the club does not currently have. This is the deadline move that changes the roster.

**Zden Chara** at OTT is the second target. 84 overall, 92 toughness, 93 checking, 98 aggressiveness, 27 years old, $1.7M, one year left. Ottawa are 10-10-2 with 11 expiring contracts. They are not a contender. Chara would want $4-5M next season on his next deal, and Ottawa has no interest at that price. He solves the toughness hole at the blue line and provides the best checking grade on the roster. $1.7M is nothing. A first-rounder gets it done.

**Shane Doan** at PHX is the third. 86 overall, 86 toughness, 91 checking, 28 years old, $2.4M, one year left. Phoenix are 9-13-4 with 14 expiring contracts and $47.81M payroll eating into only $14.26M profit. They are in a full teardown. Doan at 86 would demand $4-5M and Phoenix has $14.26M profit to spend on 14 replacements. He is a natural seller at this price and age. He fills toughness and checking on the wing alongside Bertuzzi if the club gets both.

**Kyle McLaren** at SJ is the fourth. 82 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 27 years old, $2.2M, one year left. San Jose are 9-11-2 with 14 expiring contracts and $20.71M profit. Same logic as Chara: a 27-year-old shutdown D at $2.2M expiring on a club that won't match his next salary. He is a cheaper version of Chara if the club only gets one blue-liner.

**Jason Arnott** at DAL fills the faceoff centre gap. 85 overall, 87 toughness, 80 checking, 30 years old, $3.8M, free agent after this season. Dallas are 15-9-1 and technically in the race, but their profit is only $11.47M against $66.88M payroll. If Arnott tests free agency they get zero. A first-round pick plus a cheap prospect is better than losing a 30-year-old for nothing. The trade crosses conferences (TOR East, DAL West), which removes the division-rival objection.

**Davison and Vandermeer** are depth pieces. Davison is 24, $0.5M, 86 toughness, 90 checking at SJ; Vandermeer is 24, $0.4M, 90 toughness, 88 checking at PHI. Neither moves on their own — PHI keeps a $0.4M player, and SJ has no reason to give away cheap youth. They are throw-ins in a larger deal, not standalone targets.

## Trade construction

**The question: what packages make sense to both sides, given what the coverage phase identified as thin and what the trajectory phase says we must shed?** The answer is three proposals ranked by certainty: Chara is the clean deal because Ottawa will sell, Bertuzzi is the big swing that fixes everything but faces a contending club, and Doan is the backup if Vancouver says no. None of them give a player the coach called thin.

**Chara** is the cleanest package in the league. Ottawa are 10-10-2, have 11 expiring contracts, and at $1.7M he will want $4-5M in July they won't match. A first-rounder plus a cheap forward body is market value for a seller moving an 84-overall blue-liner with 93 checking and 92 toughness. Holden is 26, $1.2M, not lined, 81 potential. They get a first-rounder and a depth forward they can keep or flip. We get the missing toughness on the blueline at 27 years old.

**Bertuzzi** is the move that changes the roster. 95 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 29, $2.6M. Vancouver are 14-8-2, which means they might say no. But Bertuzzi walks in July, and Mogilny is 39 points in 26 games right now — elite production a contending team can use for the playoff push. Toronto sheds $5.5M over two remaining years of Mogilny's deal and gets the player who makes this team physically unplayable. The risk is VAN deciding this is their year.

**Doan** at 86 overall, 86 toughness, 91 checking, 28, $2.4M fills the same forward-toughness role as Bertuzzi at lower quality. Phoenix are 9-13-4 with 14 expiring deals and $47.81M payroll eating $14.26M profit. They are selling everything. A first-rounder plus a third is fair value for a full teardown to move a top-nine winger. If Bertuzzi doesn't land, this fills the gap.

**If none land:** Tucker has 92 checking and 88 toughness at 29, $1.3M, 3 games played. He is the internal answer to both gaps and should be dressed every night. Koltsov needs to be in the lineup. The toughness problem narrows from "nobody above 80" to "one player at 88" and survives the year.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07
markdown:
# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07

Next game vs NJ on Tuesday 07 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question: is each young player getting the games and minutes his production has earned? The answer is mostly yes, but two kids are buried and one is sitting at home with nothing to show for it.

**Koltsov** is the loudest case on the sheet. 12 points in 12 games is a point a night, and he's doing it on the fourth line at 8.8 minutes. No fourth-liner out-earns that production by this much without a move. He belongs on the third line or better, and every game he spends on the fourth is a game of wasted development.

**Nash** is at 23 points in 26 games for 0.88 a night, playing 12.9 minutes on the third line. That's top-six production on third-line ice.
